summary: Championship leader Kimi Antonelli achieved a sensational victory at the Italian Grand Prix in Monza, becoming the first Italian to win the home race since 1966 after starting 19th due to grid penalties. Employing an alternative strategy and stunning pace on fresh tyres, Antonelli overtook his Mercedes team-mate George Russell in the closing laps to claim the win. Max Verstappen finished third to secure his fifth podium of the 2026 season.
key_points: Kimi Antonelli drove from 19th on the grid to win the Italian Grand Prix.
Antonelli passed Mercedes team-mate George Russell with three laps remaining to take the victory.
Max Verstappen finished in third place, holding off the McLarens to claim his fifth podium of 2026.
Charles Leclerc suffered a heavy crash on the third lap, causing a red flag.
Antonelli extended his lead in the Drivers' Championship to 66 points over Russell.

title: Odegaard and Saka star - player ratings for Arsenal v Chelsea
author: Nizaar Kinsella
content:
![Martin Odegaard celebrates his goal with Arsenal's fans](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/820/cpsprodpb/483b/live/7d606320-aa15-11f1-bbe8-51444f709166.jpg)
Martin Odegaard's winner was his second Premier League goal of the season
- Published
Captain Martin Odegaard scored the winner as Arsenal secured an impressive 2-1 home victory over Chelsea.
Club-record Â£117m signing Morgan Rogers put Chelsea ahead after just two minutes, but Kai Havertz equalised against his former club before Odegaard struck early in the second half to seal the win.
Here's how I rated the players and you can see how you scored them below.
Arsenal ratings
David Raya: The Arsenal goalkeeper was beaten by the quality of Rogers' finish but dealt comfortably with the other efforts he faced and produced one stunning save late on from Estevao. 6
Ben White: A tidy display in possession, although he made little impact at either end of the pitch. 6
Gabriel Magalhaes: Outshone by Konsa at times but still produced an effective performance. 7
Ezri Konsa: On his first Arsenal start, he won more duels than any other defender and was joint-top for possession won in the first half. 7
Riccardo Calafiori: His underlapping runs were typically adventurous and the Italy defender played a key role in creating problems from set-pieces. 7
Myles Lewis-Skelly: Fired a poor effort wide from the edge of the area late in the first half and was caught in possession in a dangerous area, but competed well in midfield. 6
Declan Rice: Played his part in a fiercely contested midfield battle and contributed well both in and out of possession. 6
Martin Odegaard: Put Arsenal ahead early in the second half with a composed finish. Also impressed with the quality of his delivery, both in open play and from set-pieces. 8
Bukayo Saka: A constant threat from set-pieces and regularly won free-kicks in dangerous positions. His impressive second-half effort was saved. 8
Kai Havertz: Passed up a shooting opportunity in the 23rd minute but made no mistake with his next chance, cutting inside to score two minutes later. Also played a part in Odegaard's goal and proved a threat at set-pieces. 7
Christos Tzolis: Delivered well from the left and provided Arsenal's main outlet whenever they broke from periods of Chelsea possession. 7
Subs:
Martin Zubimendi (on 67, Myles-Skelly): A complete substitute performance involving dangerous shots, impressive passing and breaking up the play. 7
Piero Hincapie (on 67, Calafiori): Kept it simple with Arsenal ahead. 6
Mikel Merino (on 77, Odegaard): A tidy addition late on in midfield. 6
Viktor Gyokores (on 78, Havertz): Not much opportunity to make an impact as Arsenal held onto their lead. 5
Noni Madueke (on 90, Saka)
Subs not used: Arrizabalaga, Guimaraes, Dowman
Chelsea ratings
Emiliano Martinez: There was concern when the Argentina goalkeeper was accidentally kicked in the head by Gabriel early on, but he was beaten too easily at his near post for Havertz's equaliser. He later made a high-quality save from Saka in the second half. 5
Josh Acheampong: Often dragged into uncomfortable areas by Tzolis from a tactical perspective, but handled his individual defensive duties well. 6
Maxence Lacroix: Miscontrolled a ball early on and allowed Havertz's shot to pass through his legs but also impressed at other times. 6
Wesley Fofana: Unconvincing defensively against Saka, Odegaard and, ultimately, Havertz for the equaliser, but the most composed of Chelsea's defenders in possession. 6
Pedro Neto: Tasked with marking Calafiori while also providing an attacking threat. Hit the post just before half-time with a brilliant curling effort. 7
Reece James: Saw a well-struck long-range effort saved after 22 minutes and was arguably Chelsea's best passer. 7
Romeo Lavia: Produced a superb defensive header to clear the danger in the 32nd minute and competed aggressively throughout. 6
Jorrel Hato: His determination helped create Rogers' volley and he matched that effort defensively, although he struggled to contain Saka at times. 6
Cole Palmer: Had one effort on target in the first half and was booked for a professional foul. Also had a second-half shot saved. Arsenal largely kept him quiet. 5
Morgan Rogers: Opened the scoring with a first-time volley after just two minutes. Later curled an effort narrowly wide in the 31st minute and was Chelsea's most dangerous attacking player. 7
Joao Pedro: Unconvincing defensively at set-pieces and had few opportunities in front of goal, including an ambitious effort from distance. Still made a significant contribution through his work-rate, physical presence and ability to bring team-mates into play as the number nine. 6
Subs:
Malo Gusto (on 60, Lavia): Poor effort moments after coming on, albeit playing out of position in central midfield. 5
Pep Chavarria (on 60, Hato): Struggled to track his runners on a few occasions. 6
Estevao Willian (on 80, Neto): The Brazilian's sensational curling effort almost levelled but was saved by Raya.
Danny Welbeck (on 87, Rogers)
Subs not used: Penders, Colwill, Barco, Quenda, Gittens
How did you rate the players?
Player of the match
After the opportunity to rate players has closed, the score displayed represents the average from all the submissions by BBC Sport users.
summary: Arsenal secured a 2-1 home victory over Chelsea after coming from behind in a competitive Premier League match. Morgan Rogers opened the scoring for Chelsea within the first two minutes, but Kai Havertz equalised against his former club. Captain Martin Odegaard then scored early in the second half to seal the win for Arsenal.
key_points: Morgan Rogers scored for Chelsea just two minutes into the match.
Kai Havertz equalised for Arsenal against his former club.
Martin Odegaard scored the winning goal early in the second half.
Arsenal successfully protected their lead to secure the 2-1 victory.

title: Italian Grand Prix result: Kimi Antonelli passes George Russell for stunning Monza win from 19th on grid
author: Andrew Benson
content:
![Kimi Antonelli smiles and clenches his right fist in celebration on the podium after winning the Italian Grand Prix](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1552/cpsprodpb/9aaa/live/7f6c1a00-aa07-11f1-afb5-a367f96884d3.jpg)
Kimi Antonelli is the first Italian to win at Monza since Ludovico Scarfiotti in 1966
- Published
Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli took a breathtaking victory in an incident-packed Italian Grand Prix from 19th place on the grid.
The Italian caught and passed his team-mate George Russell, who started second, with three laps to go to extend his championship lead to 66 points.
Antonelli's performance is the second furthest back a driver has ever come from to win a grand prix after John Watson's victory from 22nd on the grid in the 1983 United States Grand Prix West.
It was a statement performance from the 20-year-old, who remarkably was on Russell's tail and challenging for victory within 16 laps of the start.
Antonelli looked capable of winning any which way, but decided to stop for fresh tyres under a virtual safety car mid-race and narrowed a 15-second gap to nothing before carving past Russell.
The Italian fans, who usually support Ferrari, rose to acclaim their new hero after a sensational drive as he crossed the line to take the chequered flag.
"I did not expect," Antonelli said. "Unbelievable. I am so happy, I could never imagine being here today."
Red Bull's Max Verstappen took the final podium place ahead of the McLarens of Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri with Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton sixth.
The key stories of a gripping race at Monza were:
- Antonelli's compelling and spectacular win, the best of a stand-out season from the Italian
- A desperately disappointing day for Russell, who knew he needed to try to use this day to make up points on his team-mate
- A disappointing home race for Ferrari, with Charles Leclerc crashing out early
- A good recovery from McLaren
Antonelli again comes out on top of Mercedes battle
![Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli and George Russell side by side while battling for the lead during the Italian Grand Prix](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/4634/live/59764b50-aa01-11f1-afb5-a367f96884d3.jpg)
The Mercedes of Kimi Antonelli and George Russell repeatedly swapped positions while battling for the lead at Monza
The day started with Antonelli looking to limit the damage inflicted on his points lead by Russell as he started at the back of the grid because of a penalty for using more than his permitted number of engine parts.
An early stint of cautious, measured attacking lifted Antonelli up to 12th place on the third lap when Leclerc lost control at the Parabolica after getting slightly wide defending from Piastri, smashing deep into the barriers and bringing out the red flag.
Leclerc was unhurt and the race was stopped while the marshals rebuilt the barriers at the famous final corner.
By this time, Russell had taken the lead from shock pole winner Pierre Gasly's Alpine and looked in control of the race.
But the restart saw a compelling series of laps as the leading drivers ran nose to tail and Antonelli picked his way through the pack and into contention.
Four laps after the restart, Russell was leading a six-car train with Antonelli at the rear. Gasly started to drop back and the Italian moved past the Frenchman, Hamilton and finally Piastri before joining a three-car battle for the lead with Verstappen.
The Dutchman briefly took the lead from Russell on lap 11, before the Briton re-passed him three laps later, Antonelli overtaking the Red Bull into the second chicane.
From laps 17 to 24, the Mercedes battled hard, the two passing and re-passing each other as they played with the boost and overtaking modes in the new hybrid engines as Verstappen sat right behind them with the best seat in the house.
Antonelli was then told that Russell had been asked to push and build a gap to Verstappen, and the tension was betrayed in Antonelli's response, when he asked if they wanted him to sit back and not challenge.
Shortly afterwards, a virtual safety car was called when Lance Stroll's Aston Martin broke down at the first chicane and Antonelli's side of the garage decided to risk a stop for fresh tyres. Russell stayed out, needing to nurse his tyres to the end, and Verstappen followed Antonelli in.
Antonelli rejoined in sixth place and 15 seconds behind his team-mate, but he moved past Gasly, Norris, Hamilton and Piastri as he closed in on his team-mate.
Russell began to struggle with his tyres as Antonelli homed in and with five laps to go, the two were nose to tail.
An initial attempt into the first chicane on lap 50 came to grief when Antonelli got on to the rubber debris off line turning into the second part of the first chicane and slid into the gravel.
But such was his pace advantage that he soon closed the 1.7-second gap that had opened up and easily breezed past Russell on the run between the Lesmo corners and Ascari.
A resigned Russell said: "When I looked at the leaderboard a few laps after the restart and saw he was already in P5/6 I knew he would be in the mix. I was just struggling with the tyres at the end.
"I will take it. It has been more positive than before summer break but of course I would have loved to be P1 today."
Leclerc shattered by error as crash follows Hamilton contact
![A crane prepares to remove the Ferrari of Charles Leclerc after his heavy crash into the barriers at the Parabolica corner during the Italian Grand Prix](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1024/cpsprodpb/4459/live/00f732e0-a9f8-11f1-921b-6365210e1c9d.jpg)
A recovery vehicle removes Charles Leclerc's Ferrari after his crash into the barriers at the Parabolica
Ferrari's day to forget started when Leclerc barged Hamilton on to the grass exiting the first chicane on the opening lap, the seven-time champion dropping to 10th.
Leclerc then challenged Gasly for third on lap two before being passed by Verstappen into Ascari.
That slowed his exit, and left him vulnerable to Piastri, who attacked on the inside into Parabolica.
Leclerc was slightly wide on entry and through the apex, and that carried his left rear tyre wide onto the white line on the edge of the track, and partly over the artificial grass section before the gravel trap.
There, the car lost grip, and a high-speed tank-slapper spun Leclerc into the barrier at high-speed.
After climbing from the car, he sat down behind the barriers, his head bowed, shattered by his error.
Hamilton recovered well initially, with a strong restart moving him up to fourth within two laps.
But the Ferrari's lack of straight-line speed was ultimately costly and he slipped behind Antonelli and the McLarens as the race wore on.
![The Ferraris of Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton side by side into the first chicane at the start of the Italian Grand Prix](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/ea22/live/15bb8370-a9f8-11f1-921b-6365210e1c9d.jpg)
The Ferraris of Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton side by side at the first chicane where they collided at the start
Verstappen impressive as Norris gets Piastri at end
Everyone was put in the shade by Antonelli's superlative drive, but Verstappen was impressive in moving up from fifth on the grid to third in the Red Bull and fighting for so long with the Mercedes.
In the end, he could not hold on to the silver cars and his stop dropped him behind Piastri, Hamilton and Norris.
His fresher tyres helped him move back into third place but he could go no further.
Behind him, Norris began to move up as the race went on, and he passed Hamilton before moving on to the back of a three-car train behind Verstappen and Piastri.
Norris looked to make a move on Piastri in the closing laps but the Australian eased him over to the grass on the outside of the exit of Curve Grande as Norris went for the inside approaching the second chicane.
Norris complained he had been pushed off, and the team warned Piastri to race clean, but Norris finally did make it past on the final lap.
Gasly was never going to hold on to the lead, and the Alpine's lack of pace after his stunning qualifying performance, aided by compromises elsewhere, soon began to tell.
But seventh is a good result as Alpine went into the race aiming mainly to ensure they finished ahead of the Racing Bulls, their rivals for fifth in the constructors' championship.
Gasly succeeded, but Arvid Lindblad beat the second Alpine of Franco Colapinto to eighth place as the second Racing Bulls driver Yuki Tsunoda completed the top 10.
Is Antonelli win disrupting things for Italian fans?
Top 10
1. Kimi Antonelli (Mercedes)
2. George Russell (Mercedes)
3. Max Verstappen (Red Bull)
4. Lando Norris (McLaren)
5. Oscar Piastri (McLaren)
6. Lewis Hamilton (Ferrari)
7. Pierre Gasly (Alpine)
8. Arvid Lindblad (Racing Bulls)
9. Franco Colapinto (Alpine)
10. Yuki Tsunoda (Racing Bulls)
summary: Mercedes driver Kimi Antonelli secured a stunning victory at the Italian Grand Prix after starting 19th on the grid due to an engine penalty. He carved through the field and passed his teammate George Russell with three laps remaining to extend his championship lead. Russell finished second, while Max Verstappen took the final podium place for Red Bull.
key_points: Kimi Antonelli won the Italian Grand Prix after starting 19th on the grid, becoming the first Italian to win at Monza since 1966.
Antonelli capitalized on a mid-race virtual safety car to take fresh tires, erasing a 15-second deficit to pass teammate George Russell with three laps to go.
George Russell finished second after struggling with tire degradation in the closing stages of the race.
Max Verstappen claimed third place for Red Bull, finishing ahead of the McLarens of Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri.
Ferrari suffered a disappointing home race, highlighted by Charles Leclerc crashing out early after losing control at the Parabolica.

title: How Gasly and Alpine beat Mercedes, Ferrari, McLaren and Red Bull to Italian GP pole
author: Stuart Codling
content:
![Pierre Gasly, Alpine](https://cdn-1.motorsport.com/images/amp/YE9EKeDY/s1000/pierre-gasly-alpine.webp) 
How Gasly and Alpine beat Mercedes, Ferrari, McLaren and Red Bull to Italian GP pole
Superior execution by both team and driver enabled Pierre Gasly to edge past cars that have been faster all season
Revenge is a dish best served on a hot Monza afternoon. A day after being “robbed” (his words, to Canal+) of his Monaco Formula 1 podium, Pierre Gasly claimed his first career pole at the track where he registered his sensational maiden victory in 2020.
It wasn’t just a case of beating George Russell by 0.060s on a day when Mercedes only had one car in the mix for pole, owing to Kimi Antonelli’s grid penalty for adding a new power unit to the pool.
Gasly also saw off cars that might not have been outright pole contenders, but which have made his Alpine A526 at best a fringe player for top-10 finishes over the balance of the 2026 season. Having a Mercedes power unit helped, of course, as did better understanding of the latest upgrade package applied at Zandvoort, but this was a triumph of execution.
“Our expectation on our performance tracker had us going into Q3 and being 8th, 9th, 10th,” said Alpine managing director Steve Nielsen. “We got everything out of the car. So, honestly, we didn't expect this, but of course we'll take it.”
To unpick how Gasly and Alpine did a better job, we need to examine how the latest technical regulations have complicated what has always been a difficult proposition at the home of the Italian Grand Prix.
The value of the tow
Since Tazio Nuvolari was in short trousers, getting an aerodynamic ‘tow’ from the car in front at Monza has ranged between a valuable leg-up and a nice-to-have, critical only in unusual circumstances, as in 1992 when Ayrton Senna helped his countryman Mauricio Gugelmin scrape on to the grid in the miserably under-powered Jordan-Yamaha. This season, the huge contribution of the electrical motor to total power output has made a tow at Monza nothing less than utterly necessary.
Getting into the slipstream of the car ahead requires you to use fractionally less battery power, which pays back in the form of delaying the inevitable “staircase” as electrical deployment ramps down in stages as the charge depletes. This is just one facet in the overall mix, but it complicates the approach to all the other prerequisites for a strong lap time in a current F1 car.
![While some teams struggled to set up a tow, Alpine's drivers stuck together](https://cdn.motorsport.com/images/mgl/6lmAVDL0/s1000/lewis-hamilton-ferrari-pierre-.jpg) 
While some teams struggled to set up a tow, Alpine's drivers stuck together
Photo by: Manuel Eletto / Getty Images
Take the out-lap: all the usual tyre preparation and battery charging has to be completed with part of the driver and pitwall’s mental bandwidth directed towards synchronising all this with the opportunity for a tow. All this while bringing the brakes up to temperature – difficult when the biggest braking areas come early in the lap, and cycling through acceleration and braking phases later on the out-lap could cost battery power.
Once in the lap, the nature of this track demands utmost precision: corner speed has to be optimum. Again, the demands of power management have added to the challenges of assembling a lap.
It’s not necessarily a case of driving to the limits of adhesion, more a balance between avoiding scrubbing off speed through understeering into the corner or letting the rear step out at the exit – because all that lost momentum has to be recouped out of the electrical energy budget, giving less to ‘spend’ on those long straights. Every tiny slip comes back in the form of the algorithm turning off the taps that little bit earlier. At an energy-starved track such as this, there are innumerable ways of leaking lap time.
Hence the importance of the tow. And, with it, team discipline. The temptation to ‘accidentally’ fail to give a team-mate that vital leg up is powerful here, especially when there are big rewards at stake. Let’s not forget Charles Leclerc’s landmark victory here in 2019 from a pole position gifted to him via a tow from Sebastian Vettel – which Leclerc didn’t reciprocate. In F1, agreements between team-mates aren’t worth the paper they aren’t written on – unless the boss is prepared to wield the rod.
Teamwork
The auguries were there all through qualifying if you studied the live GPS trace as the sessions unfolded. Unfailingly, Gasly and team-mate Franco Colapinto towed each other around neatly, while Gasly was also able to duck into the slipstream of other cars ahead. This is a factor of sharp pitwall operations and good communication as well as the driver seizing the moment.
In contrast, Ferrari barely managed to get its cars out in proximity to each other at the same time, seemingly too fixated on big-picture hardpoints such as saving tyres in Q2 and ensuring total equality between drivers to react improvisationally in the moment. Given events more recent than Leclerc/Vettel in 2019 – the failure to implement team orders promptly at Zandvoort two weeks ago springs to mind – this is perhaps to be expected.
Ferrari’s execution was off throughout, as Leclerc suffered battery issues in Q2, which team boss Frederic Vasseur put down to him not getting enough charge on his out-lap. Lewis Hamilton only escaped Q2 by a millisecond, denied only by Audi’s Gabriel Bortoleto having a moment on his final run. Then the Briton was left running on his own in his first Q3 run – according to him, because the wheels hadn’t yet been put on his car while everyone else was leaving the pits.
![Max Verstappen was without wingman Liam Lawson in Q3](https://cdn.motorsport.com/images/mgl/0kZXQ8D6/s1000/max-verstappen-red-bull-racing.jpg) 
Max Verstappen was without wingman Liam Lawson in Q3
Photo by: Andy Hone/ LAT Images via Getty Images
“We do work as a team, but have we been?” mused Hamilton. “What I can say is, Pierre did a great job. But clearly, looking from a distance, it looked like they [Alpine] worked really well as a team.”
If Ferrari, despite the latest Additional Development and Upgrade Opportunities (ADUO) tweaks to the turbo, needed to execute perfectly to be in with a chance of beating Mercedes to pole, McLaren and Red Bull didn’t have the outright pace to get there and needed others ahead to fail. Instead, they contrived to shoot themselves in the foot.
Max Verstappen arrived in Q3 without his wingman, Liam Lawson having been eliminated in Q2. Red Bull had fitted Lawson’s car with a new power unit, which would have incurred a grid penalty, but then failed to get him into a proper tow.
Hence Lawson’s expletive-laden radio message saying the team had “hung me out to dry”. Although Oscar Piastri impeded Lawson on his final Q2 lap – and lost three grid spots for doing so – Lawson was already swinging in the breeze on the washing line by then.
That left Verstappen needing the charity of others for a tow, or running an interference line to scupper somebody else’s lap. He chose the latter, infuriating Russell by trying to get between the two Mercedes at the end of their out-laps on the final Q3 runs.
Not that the “papier-Wache” Red Bull would have been a contender for pole anyway, but the Dutchman could have expected to be ahead of Gasly on the grid.
Ditto McLaren. Monza wasn’t expected to favour the MCL40, given its aero efficiency deficit to Mercedes as well as its marginal brakes. But while Piastri, with a tow from Norris, strung together a first Q3 run good enough for third until his penalty, holding up Lawson was sloppy.
![Piastri screwed his own qualifying by impeding Lawson, then did the same to Norris by locking up in Turn 1 and denying him a tow](https://cdn.motorsport.com/images/mgl/YXyK1Kj6/s1000/oscar-piastri-mclaren.jpg) 
Piastri screwed his own qualifying by impeding Lawson, then did the same to Norris by locking up in Turn 1 and denying him a tow
Photo by: Simon Galloway / LAT Images via Getty Images
He then speared off at Turn 1 on the final Q3 runs when he was supposed to be giving Lando Norris a tow. Accidental or Leclerc 2019-style Machiavellian shenanigans? Either way, Norris ended up without a tow since the McLarens were running at the head of the field. He had also been too far behind Russell at the start of his first Q3 run to get a reasonable tow down the main straight.
The blunder at the end of Q3, team boss Andrea Stella explained, was partly a function of their garage’s position at the pit entry rather than exit. This gives a cleaner entry during race pitstops but made the timing of the final Q3 runs dicey. Leave it too late and they ran the risk of being at the back of the queue, perhaps even missing out on a final push lap if the chequered flag came out before they crossed the line. In the end they went too soon.
“Overall, there are multiple areas in which we have not executed at the level that we should have,” rued Stella afterwards. “Because in Monza, which is so peculiar, position of the car on track is as important as the underlying car performance. And also, the management of the power unit and the brakes is, once again, as important as these other factors. So, there was more that we could have achieved.”
Gasly vs Russell
If Ferrari ultimately took itself out of the equation for pole, Russell’s second Q3 run, which Gasly beat by 0.060s, is slightly trickier to decipher. Comparing the Briton’s first and second runs – the first one of 1m21.929s being good enough for provisional pole – suggests a big difference in deployment over the second half of the lap.
On his second run, Russell lost about half a second overall through the first chicane compared with his first, where he was later off the throttle and on the brakes from a slightly higher top speed, then neater on the throttle at the exit.
Towards the second chicane on that final run, he was marginally quicker on top speed, but then built to a peak of around 10km/h faster than his previous run on the straight between the Lesmos and Ascari, then again between Ascari and Parabolica. This is where he pulled back the time he lost at Turn 1 and more, despite carrying too much speed into Ascari and having to dodge an appointment with the run-off.
![Gasly nailed his final Q3 lap as everyone else faltered](https://cdn.motorsport.com/images/mgl/6x7LKZ8Y/s1000/pierre-gasly-alpine.jpg) 
Gasly nailed his final Q3 lap as everyone else faltered
Photo by: Andy Hone/ LAT Images via Getty Images
Russell felt he was impeded by Verstappen on his final run, but was he?
"We had a bit of a mess with Verstappen entering the lap," he said. "Everything was all looking fine but then going into Parabolica, Max just slammed on the brakes and he didn't want to be the lead car. It's just one of those things, you know, you can't control what other people do. Kimi was there to give me the slipstream, which he did perfectly on the first run. But obviously with Max, I think it also made it difficult for Kimi to know what to do as well. So, it was just a little bit unfortunate. I did my lap a second and a half behind Max, which wasn't ideal."
These claims don’t quite stack up. Earlier on Saturday, the Mercedes had been rehearsing the tow between them all the way to the second chicane. On Russell’s first Q3 run Antonelli dived out of the way well before the braking area for the first chicane. Russell then had no tow for the rest of the lap. On the second run, Verstappen did cause Russell to check up before the Parabolica – it’s there in the data and the onboard footage – but although that prompted Antonelli to dive out of the way almost immediately on the front straight, Russell still had the benefit of Verstappen making a hole in the air ahead.
So, while Russell clearly paid the price for being discombobulated by Verstappen’s spoiler tactics in terms of his confidence under braking for Turn 1 (and then being fractionally too aggressive on the throttle at the exit, requiring a brief correction), the benefits of having a slipsteam from the Red Bull driver later on in the lap are clear.
Gasly got a cleaner exit from the opening chicane, carried more speed through the second, had a higher apex speed at both Lesmos, and had a quicker overall trajectory through the Parabolica. Enjoying a tow from Hamilton (who in turn had a tow from Leclerc, who was in the slipstream of Arvid Lindblad) enabled him to ameliorate losses arising from Mercedes’ straightline speed advantage over the slightly draggier Alpine.
So, it was a combination of being in the right place at the right time, thanks to on-point teamwork, and then pressing that advantage home. Team-mate Colapinto could have joined him at the sharp end but he lost a little too much ground while warming his tyres on the back straight during his out-lap, so he was fractionally too distant to enjoy an optimal tow.
“We knew that there was a bit more on the table in the practice sessions and then I think it was a very good execution from the team, always putting me in a great position on track, managing the gap as best we could,” explained Gasly. “So, I think my last lap, managed to target, you know, slightly over 2.5 seconds behind Lewis when he was going to be fast and sort of, like, drag me with him. So, I think it was perfect execution. It’s not down to one simple parameter. I think everybody did a very good job and we’ve been rewarded for it.”
![Can Gasly convert pole into victory?](https://cdn.motorsport.com/images/mgl/YvKBPbG6/s1000/pierre-gasly-alpine.jpg) 
Can Gasly convert pole into victory?
Photo by: Bryn Lennon / Formula 1 via Getty Images
Subscribe and access Autosport.com with your ad-blocker.
From Formula 1 to MotoGP we report straight from the paddock because we love our sport, just like you. In order to keep delivering our expert journalism, our website uses advertising. Still, we want to give you the opportunity to enjoy an ad-free and tracker-free website and to continue using your adblocker.
summary: Pierre Gasly claimed a surprise pole position for the Italian Grand Prix at Monza, edging out George Russell by 0.60 seconds through superior teamwork and execution. While Alpine's drivers worked seamlessly together to manage crucial aerodynamic tows and power deployment, rival teams like Ferrari, McLaren, and Red Bull suffered from strategic blunders and poor execution. Despite various complications and rival tactical interference, Gasly delivered a flawless final lap to secure his first career pole.
key_points: Pierre Gasly secured pole position at Monza by beating George Russell by 0.060 seconds.
Alpine successfully utilized team discipline and synchronized tows between Gasly and Franco Colapinto to maximize performance.
Rival teams including Ferrari, McLaren, and Red Bull faltered due to poor coordination, strategic mistakes, and missed tow opportunities.
Maximizing aerodynamic tows and managing electrical battery deployment were critical factors on the energy-starved Monza circuit under current regulations.

title: Arsenal vs. Chelsea, Premier League: Preview, team news, how to watch
author: David Pasztor
content:
In the Premier Parity League, only four teams have come through the first two weeks without dropping points. After this weekend, there can only be two as two of them will meet at the Emirates on Sunday for a good old fashioned battle for London Supremacy.
Arsenal broke their 22-year title drought last season. In those intervening two decades, Chelsea had won the Premier League five times: the only London club to do so. (Sadly, the last of those is now a decade old itself.) Chelsea’s rise to the top starting in 2004 was a symbolic and very real shift in power, dethroning the “Invincibles” who had won the league without losing a game the prior season. London was Blue.
It is now red again. Can we take it back? We can’t do so with just one game, but it would be a great start, especially considering that we’ve failed to beat them in eleven (11!) straight in all competitions, losing eight.
Only two teams seem to be rising above the parity in this early season, Arsenal and Manchester City. We are trying to get back into that elite group. Here’s a great chance to show those ambitions.
Date / Time: Sunday, September 6, 2026, 16.30 BST; 11:30am EDT; 9pm IST
Venue: Emirates Stadium, London
Referee: Chris Kavanagh (on pitch); Darren England (VAR)
Forecast: Sunny and quite warm; all the UV you’d ever want
On TV: Sky Sports Main Event (UK); USA, Telemundo (USA); Star Sports Select HD1 (India); Canal+ (NGA); elsewhere
Streaming: Sky Go (UK), NBC Sports Live, Telemundo Deportes En Vivo (USA); JioHotstar (India); DStv Now (NGA)
![LONDON COLNEY, ENGLAND - SEPTEMBER 03: Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta talks with defender Ben White during a training session at Sobha Realty Training Centre on September 03, 2026 in London Colney, England. (Photo by Stuart MacFarlane/Arsenal FC via Getty Images)](https://platform.weaintgotnohistory.sbnation.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/178/2026/09/gettyimages-2293350484.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&crop=0%2C0%2C100%2C100&w=2400)
Arsenal team news: The Gunners won the league with just 85 points last season, one of the lowest winning totals in the 21st century. The 71 goals they scored was the second lowest total for the champions after Leicester City’s 68. It was a title built on defending and set pieces — they briefly flirted with Chelsea’s (surely unbeatable) record for fewest goals conceded in a season — and that’s the plan for this season as well. They are one of only two teams to not concede a goal so far.
As all good champions should, Arsenal approached the transfer window from a position of strength, adding proven talent in Bruno Guimarães from Newcastle and Ezri Konsa from Aston Villa, plus a promising young winger in Christos Tzolis from Club Brugge, who’s really caught the eye these first two weeks. Departing were the likes of Gabriel Martinelli, Gabriel Jesus, and the ever-annoying Leandro Trossard. Christian Nørgaard’s also left the team, after barely featuring in his twelve months there. All the former Chelsea crew are still around, including Kai Havertz, Noni Madueke, Declan Rice, and even Kepa Arrizabalaga (despite the arrival of another perpetually underwhelming backup goalkeeper in Illan Meslier).
Rice and Bruno are among those who are dealing with minor knocks already (but are probable to play), while Cristhian Mosquera and Jurrien Timber face late fitness tests. Key defender William Saliba remains out with the back injury he sustained in the World Cup semifinal against Spain.
![COBHAM, ENGLAND - SEPTEMBER 3: Manager Xabi Alonso of Chelsea during a training session at Chelsea Training Ground on September 3, 2026 in Cobham, United Kingdom. (Photo by Darren Walsh/Chelsea FC via Getty Images)](https://platform.weaintgotnohistory.sbnation.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/178/2026/09/gettyimages-2292750708.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&crop=0%2C0%2C100%2C100&w=2400)
Chelsea team news: The big injury question for the Blues is the status of Moisés Caicedo. He had missed the first two games before coming off the bench in the second half last weekend. Unfortunately, his day would last just 13 minutes, and he remains questionable for tomorrow. Valentín Barco finished out the game in his stead, and would likely be called upon in what is expected to be a feisty encounter.
In the absences of Caicedo and Enzo Fernández (who’s now gone to Manchester City), Xabi Alonso has cobbled together a midfield from the likes of Roméo Lavia, Reece James, and Malo Gusto (not a typo), hoping that they would be able to hold own the center well enough for the front three (and the wing-backs) to combine and do their thing. This plan has worked in some ways (seven goals scored), and not worked in other ways (five conceded). Alonso’s not one to preach possession for possession’s sake, but we’ve been made to pay for our lack of control at times, and it’s probably not a sustainable approach to have to keep putting up 3-4 goals per game even with the talents Cole Palmer, João Pedro, and Morgan Rogers (and even if we now have less of a wild card in goal, at least slightly, in former Arsenal man Emi Martínez instead of Rob Sánchez).
Chelsea spent much of transfer deadline day trying to add to our midfield options, but after AS Monaco’s shenanigans over Lamine Camara, we were left with nothing. Arsenal’s Martín Zubimendi was among those who had been considered earlier in the window, but the Gunners rejected even the faintest notions of any such move. We did sign Jordan Henderson to maybe help out in that regard (and in terms of some much needed leadership), but he’s still not fit to play. Wing-back Marco Palestra also remains out, for at least a few more days, after picking up an injury at the end of preseason.
Previously: It’s been five years since we won at the Emirates, when Romelu Lukaku scored. Feels like two lifetimes ago. We played four times last season, and all four were close games: a draw at the Bridge, a one-goal defeat at the Emirates, plus two one-goal defeats in either leg of the League Cup semifinal. But close only counts in horseshoes and hand grenades, as they say.
summary: Arsenal and Chelsea will face off at the Emirates Stadium on Sunday in an early-season Premier League clash between two of the four teams that have won their first two matches. Arsenal enters the fixture on an eleven-game unbeaten run against Chelsea in all competitions and has yet to concede a goal this season. Meanwhile, Chelsea is managing several midfield concerns, including fitness questions surrounding Moisés Caicedo and Jordan Henderson.
key_points: The match takes place on Sunday, September 6, 2026, at the Emirates Stadium.
Arsenal has not lost to Chelsea in their last eleven matches across all competitions, winning eight of them.
Arsenal enters the match as one of only two teams yet to concede a goal this season.
Chelsea's squad faces fitness doubts for Moisés Caicedo, while Jordan Henderson remains unfit to play.
Chris Kavanagh will referee the match, with Darren England serving as the VAR official.

title: Haaland edges Manchester City past Coventry as Fernández sparkles on debut
author: Jamie Jackson
content:
Enzo Fernández started for Manchester City after Nico O’Reilly’s back injury during the warm-up and sparkled, showing why the club paid a British-record-equalling £125m for the midfielder. The winner came courtesy of Erling Haaland’s 300th goal in club football and Fernández had a key part, feeding Antoine Semenyo, whose cross from the right was crashed home.
In the second half Coventry hammered away, but their wait for a first top-flight goal since Mustapha Hadji’s second in a 3-2 defeat at Aston Villa on 5 May 2001 goes on. The visitors did not like losing, but were heartened by holding the star-studded hosts to a slender win, though the bottom line is all three of their Premier League outings on their return have been defeats.
Frank Lampard said: “I don’t think we deserved to lose. I’m disappointed we didn’t get what we deserved – which was a point. We can walk out of here with our heads held extremely high.”
Enzo Maresca’s men have a maximum nine points so can be supremely satisfied. “Today was not a nice win, a bit ugly,” he said. “In the first half we deserved more goals – we scored one but could have scored one or two more.”
The manager said of Fernández: “The reason Enzo was on the bench [initially] was because he arrived only a few days ago. I know how frustrating it was for him in the last weeks but in the end he played some minutes and was quite good. Nico felt something in his back – not serious.”
Ayyoub Bouaddi, bought for £85m, was on the bench for the hosts, as Fernández lined up alongside Rayan Cherki in a 4-1-2–2-1 that had Semenyo and Iliman Ndiaye, another new home signing, stationed behind Haaland.
![Enzo Fernández shoots on his Manchester City debut](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/a08a8afd6e0d0f4fd500f56589dca65db0c3981b/0_0_3666_2280/master/3666.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Coventry, with Ethan Pinnock and Frank Onyeka replacing Caleb Yirenkyi and Loum Tchaouna from the XI that lost at home to Hull, could have taken the lead when Abdukodir Khusanov played the ball back to Gianluigi Donnarumma and it slipped under the goalkeeper’s boot, but the Italian scrambled it clear. The visitors should then have bridged the 25 years to Hadji when a Semenyo pass meant for Rúben Dias was intercepted by Taiwo Awoniyi. But when the striker ran in his radar failed, and the shot was pulled wide.
The longer Coventry stayed level the better their prospects. Cherki fed a galloping Haaland and he twisted and let fly, but Carl Rushworth’s save was equal to the shot. Then, dazzling Cherki footwork – after a pass from Fernández – was followed by an effort that struck a post.
The frame of the goal and Rushworth could do nothing to stop Haaland’s opener. This time Fernández curved a pass in behind for Semenyo, the right-winger spun the ball over, and Haaland did the rest.
This was 26 minutes in and Coventry were under siege. Fernández collected the ball along the right, looked up and aimed a cross for Haaland but it failed to beat the first man. Then Cherki, again in Fred Astaire mode, made space and saw an effort blocked.
Maresca wants his wingers to be more direct – utilising the pace of Ndiaye and Semenyo – and the tactic spun Coventry. So, too, did an impish Cherki flick which put Haaland in again: he rode a challenge when going down might have brought a penalty, before shooting. Rushworth once more thwarted the Norwegian.
after newsletter promotion
![Frank Lampard and the Coventry players applaud their fans](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/b3f38a9a788e99dbd1b0bb249bf0da17fec78bfb/0_0_4973_3093/master/4973.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
For Coventry, Jack Rudoni did better than Awoniyi with a header at close range, but Donnarumma flew to his left to prevent an equaliser. This showed the hope Lampard’s men carried but they had to finish any chance as these were scarce.
Ndiaye was fairly quiet on debut and when Cherki’s work took the ball to him in the area he should have pulled the trigger but refused.
Maresca said of the Senegalese: “Ili just had two sessions with us – most of the time he was moving in the wrong way, he needs to learn. When Marc Guéhi has the ball [at centre-back] he was dropping a lot – we didn’t need that, we needed him in the final third, that space was for Josko [Gvardiol, the left-back].”
The manager was more enthused about Elliot Anderson. “Really impressed not just today, he was very good against Palace, and against Bournemouth,” said Maresca. “The best thing with Elliot is day by day he wants to be better.”
Bouaddi’s home debut came on 75 minutes for Fernández and the 18-year-old showed composure during Coventry’s late-game bombardment, which included Ellis Sims forcing a point-blank save from Donnarumma.
summary: Manchester City defeated Coventry 1-0 thanks to Erling Haaland's 300th club goal, which came from an Antoine Semenyo cross initiated by debutant Enzo Fernández. Fernández started after replacing Nico O’Reilly, who suffered a back injury in the warm-up. Despite a strong second-half effort from Coventry, Enzo Maresca's side secured their third consecutive Premier League victory, while Coventry remained winless on their return to the top flight.
key_points: Enzo Fernández made his debut for Manchester City following a late warm-up injury to Nico O’Reilly.
Erling Haaland scored his 300th club career goal to secure the 1-0 win for Manchester City.
Coventry suffered their third defeat in as many Premier League outings since returning to the top flight.
Manager Frank Lampard stated that Coventry deserved a point from the match despite the loss.

title: Nottingham Forest 0-0 Tottenham: Expensive but misfiring Spurs still need to improve
author: Nick Mashiter
content:
![Scoreboard of Nottingham Forest 0-0 Tottenham](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1024/cpsprodpb/8c40/live/c9c55f00-a94c-11f1-ae8c-2528accc9a1a.jpg)
Tottenham scored five against Charlton in the League Cup but are yet to score in the top flight this season
- Published
It has been more than half a century since Tottenham have gone this long without a league goal to start the season.
A City Ground stalemate at Nottingham Forest at least gets Roberto de Zerbi's side their first point of the season but not to the extent they would want.
It followed defeats to Brentford and Newcastle which means Spurs have failed to score in their opening three league games for the first time since 1974-75.
Spurs did not play badly - they were the better side - but after their huge summer transfer outlay more is needed and expected.
De Zerbi preached patience and he is right - 10 senior arrivals means his team is still to find an identity.
And they did leave Forest with a point, something they have failed to do for almost three years.
Indeed, the video assistant referee's call to rule out Neco Williams' bundled second-half effort ensured it was not a third-straight Premier League defeat for Spurs.
Yet they have now failed to score in three successive Premier League games for the first time since November 2021, and improvement is needed at misfiring Spurs.
Forest and Spurs still looking for first win after 0-0 draw
Last March's 3-0 win for Forest at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium provided the platform for the visitors' survival bid while leaving Spurs floundering until the final day.
Since then Spurs have spent over Â£300m on new players - contributing to the record Â£3.49bn Premier League outlay this summer.
Sandro Tonali, Jon Paul Van Hecke, Savio and Omar Marmoush were the new signings who started on Saturday, with De Zerbi remaining calm after another blank.
"We bought very, very good players but you can't just build the team with the names like in Football Manager," he told Sky Sports.
"We are disappointed for the result but for the performance very happy. Considering we started to work together last Thursday for the first time, for the first day.
"We have to improve in every part of football, organisation with and without the ball. Even today I thought we defended very well.
"We have to work because I think we played very well with the ball, we found the solution. I think we can be much better in the final third."
De Zerbi bemoaned Tottenham's decision-making with Marmoush a culprit, blazing over in the second half with Andy Robertson on an overlap and Mohammed Kudus waiting for a far-post tap in.
The former Brighton boss could see the positives but needs his men to discover their composure.
"I think we played well, in the last third we have to improve, we have to take better decisions, maybe keep calmer when we are close to doing something important.
"The chance when Marmoush shot, we had Robertson overlapping. If we take the right decision and if we play with Robertson on the second post there is Kudus to score.
"I am very happy with the spirit, with the organisation, their style of play is very clear, long ball and second ball, even the second ball we won many duels. They are good players.
"Taking a point in this stadium is not so easy. We are not happy because we didn't win but this is the right spirit and the right way to move on in this moment."
A draw was Tottenham's eighth in the league this year, their most across a calendar year since 2020, and they failed to have a shot on target in a top-flight match for the first time since April 2022 against Brentford under Antonio Conte.
Spurs have had 38 shots in the league this season with an expected goals of 3.3 and former midfielder Danny Murphy agreed with De Zerbi over what the visitors lacked.
"When Spurs did get in really good areas, they just rushed it and shot when they maybe should've passed," he told BBC Sport.
"They made the wrong choice on pullbacks or crosses when they're getting in wide areas, taking men on one too many times when they've already got the space.
"They were just missing that little bit of calmness and composure that you expect from top quality players.
"It takes time for some players [to find chemistry]. You could argue that Marmoush and Savio know each other anyway and bright footballers quickly learn each other's runs and movements.
"From a midfielder to a forward perspective, you're not always sure what they're going to do. Whereas if you played with someone for a while, it comes more naturally. So those relationships will build."
De Zerbi post match reaction
Mudryk makes his Premier League return
![Mykhailo Mudryk](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1024/cpsprodpb/f82d/live/af6e46f0-a94a-11f1-ae8c-2528accc9a1a.jpg)
Mykhailo Mudryk played his first competitive game in 646 days
Mykhailo Mudryk arrived on deadline day, on an initial loan from Chelsea, looking to revive his career following his four-year ban for testing positive for banned substance meldonium in 2024, something he denied knowingly ingesting.
The Ukraine international came off the bench, his first Premier League appearance since being a second-half substitute in a 1-1 draw against Arsenal in November 2024.
"He needs time and he needs work, we have in that position Mathys Tel - big potential - but also Tel takes too many wrong decisions," added De Zerbi.
"Two big players with potential."
It was part of a second-half shake-up with Savio and Destiny Udogie being withdrawn after an hour in a planned double substitution on medical advice.
De Zerbi added: "Before the game the plan for Savio and Udogie was around 60 minutes. I'm not happy but football is like this, Savio not in the best physical condition to play 90 mins, he's a crucial player for us.
"Destiny is another crucial player. Kudus and Robertson played well but to start one game like today is not so easy to come inside from the bench and adapt immediately.
"I'm not happy when we have the plan but it's not my business, the management of players after injuries."
summary: Tottenham played out a 0-0 draw against Nottingham Forest to secure their first point of the Premier League season, but they remain without a top-flight goal. Following a significant summer transfer outlay, manager Roberto de Zerbi's side is still searching for an identity and needs to improve in the final third. The match also marked Mykhailo Mudryk's return to the Premier League as a substitute following a ban.
key_points: Tottenham have failed to score in their opening three league games for the first time since the 1974-75 season.
Manager Roberto de Zerbi preached patience following a summer transfer outlay of over £300m that brought 10 senior arrivals.
A VAR review ruling out Neco Williams' second-half effort prevented Tottenham from suffering a third consecutive Premier League defeat.
Mykhailo Mudryk made his first Premier League appearance in 646 days after coming off the bench for his debut following a drug ban.

title: Nottingham Forest boss Oliver Glasner angry with VAR handball call
author: Chris McKenna; Dale Johnson
content:
Forest and Spurs still looking for first win after 0-0 draw
- Published
Nottingham Forest manager Oliver Glasner claimed the video assistant referee (VAR) was "guessing" and should not have intervened in ruling out Neco Williams' goal in their 0-0 draw with Tottenham.
Williams' second-half effort was chalked off with the full-back adjudged to have bundled the ball in with his arm after some calamitous Tottenham defending at the City Ground.
The Forest defender denied it came off his arm and insisted it should have stood.
Initially, referee Craig Pawson awarded the goal but VAR Peter Bankes intervened.
"I watched five or six different angles and, to be fair, from one angle you can guess that the ball touched the arm because the shirt moves a little bit, but it's not clear is it the ball or [Sandro] Tonali on the goalline," said Glasner.
"I think the VAR can't intervene when he is guessing. It was not clear and obvious.
"We had a briefing before the season that the threshold for VAR intervention this year should be very high, which is why this is a wrong intervention.
"If it's not 100% clear, stick to the on-field decisions. This is the inconsistency today.
"I told the referee after the game that I felt the goal should have stood."
The Premier League's official match centre posted on their X page, external the explanation as to why it was ruled out following the incident in the 67th minute.
It stated: "VAR checked the referee's call of goal to Nottingham Forest - and determined that Williams handled the ball immediately before scoring and recommended that the goal was disallowed."
The rule states that if the ball has hit the arm of the goalscorer immediately before they score then it must be ruled out, even if accidental.
However, Williams denied that it struck his arm amid the chaos in the Spurs box.
"It's a goal," the Forest full-back told Sky Sports.
"VAR is there when there is a clear and obvious error and for me that is not clear and obvious. I've seen the images and the replays and at not one moment did I think I handballed it. I headed it in between my arms.
"I knew straight away I've headed it down in between my arms. At a loss at that one. Disappointing."
'It should have been a goal' - Glasner on disallowed goal
Analysis: This is not about a clear and obvious error
The biggest issue with judging handball is often determining if the ball did actually hit the arm, and that is the crux of Forest's argument.
Williams is adamant the ball came off his head and did not touch his hand, evidence which of course would not be available to the VAR.
Even having a chip in the ball, like at the World Cup, would not help here as the head and hands were so close together.
This is not about a clear and obvious error, as that covers subjective incidents like potential penalties.
It is a factual overturn so the VAR, Bankes, is looking for definitive proof. This is similar but without taking into account what the referee, Pawson, says he has seen.
Definitive proof can be seen as a higher bar than clear and obvious, because it is a factual decision - that the ball definitely touched the goalscorer's arm.
Glasner, Williams and most of the Forest fanbase refuse to accept that evidence does exist, and that there were no grounds to disallow the goal.
These decisions come down to one factor - the judgement of who is in the VAR room on a given match.
It is unavoidable that another VAR on a different day might feel the threshold of proof had not been crossed, and allow the goal to stand.
And this will always be one of the major frustrations with VAR.
Harry Maguire's goal against Ipswich last weekend was allowed despite a handball because his shot was going wide before it was deflected, meaning it was an own goal.
In the Williams' case, he actually was the goalscorer so any touch on the arm means the goal must be ruled out.
The only thing that would have saved the goal was if the ball had fully crossed the line before it was kicked against Williams.
summary: Nottingham Forest manager Oliver Glasner expressed frustration after VAR intervened to disallow Neco Williams' second-half goal in a 0-0 draw against Tottenham. The goal was ruled out because officials judged that the ball struck Williams' arm immediately before he scored. Both Glasner and Williams argued that the decision lacked definitive proof and failed to meet the threshold for overturning an on-field decision.
key_points: Nottingham Forest and Tottenham played out a 0-0 draw at the City Ground.
Manager Oliver Glasner criticized VAR Peter Bankes for intervening and "guessing" on a factual handball decision.
Neco Williams denied that the ball touched his arm, insisting he scored with his head.
Match officials ruled out the 67th-minute goal because rules state any accidental handball by a goalscorer immediately before scoring must be disallowed.

title: F1 Italian GP: Gasly takes stunning maiden pole for Alpine
author: Filip Cleeren
content:
F1 Italian GP: Gasly takes stunning maiden pole for Alpine
Alpine's Pierre Gasly shocks the frontrunners to take his first-ever Formula 1 pole position at the Italian Grand Prix
![Pierre Gasly, Alpine](https://cdn-7.motorsport.com/images/amp/YvKBPbG6/s1000/pierre-gasly-alpine-3.webp) 
Pierre Gasly, Alpine
Photo by: Bryn Lennon / Formula 1 via Getty Images
On the scene of his maiden grand prix win, Alpine driver Pierre Gasly has written another chapter in his Formula 1 career by claiming his first-ever pole position for the Italian Grand Prix.
In a thrilling Q3 shootout, Gasly trumped pre-session favourite George Russell by a mere 0.060s to deny the Mercedes driver a fifth pole of the year and take Alpine to the top of the timesheets.
Russell had drawn first blood in the final shootout with a 1m21.929s lap, ahead of Oscar Piastri, Gasly and Charles Leclerc.
With the entire top 10 covered by less than two tenths, getting optimal track position to benefit from a slipstream proved crucial, with Russell having an ace up his sleeve in the shape of team-mate Kimi Antonelli.
Antonelli is set to start on the last row due to an engine penalty, so the Italian was asked to tow Russell around the 5.8km track.
But Gasly also played his cards to perfection by grabbing a slipstream from Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton, and delivered an outstanding lap to leapfrog Russell.
![Pierre Gasly, Alpine](https://cdn.motorsport.com/images/mgl/6x7LKZ8Y/s1000/pierre-gasly-alpine.jpg) 
Pierre Gasly, Alpine
Photo by: Andy Hone/ LAT Images via Getty Images
Piastri and Leclerc were third and fourth, followed by Hamilton and Max Verstappen. Antonelli was seventh but will lose that position on the grid, elevating Franco Colapinto to seventh.
Norris was a disappointed ninth after not being able to grab a slipstream from team-mate Piastri, who went off in Turn 1. In doing so, the Australian ruined his own lap and left Norris punching a hole in the air by himself. Piastri and Norris had both struggled under brakes in Turn 1, and Piastri is also expected to be investigated for blocking Liam Lawson.
Arvid Lindblad qualified 10th and will move up to ninth as a result of Antonelli's penalty.
The first barrage of Q2 runs left Ferrari's Hamilton in the drop zone, appearing to catch traffic at the wrong time on his run, which left the seven-time world champion with a lot of work to do on his final run.
With Leclerc also under pressure in ninth, neither team-mate was in a position to help the other red car. Leclerc was unable to improve his lap, but Hamilton did manage to wrangle half a tenth out of the SF-26, demoting Audi's Gabriel Bortoleto by a minuscule 0.001s margin and sparing the Scuderia's blushes.
Bortoleto was followed out by Haas' Oliver Bearman, who used an upgraded car and power unit to take 12th. An unhappy Lawson was eliminated in 13th, denying Red Bull a chance to give Verstappen a tow in Q3.
![Charles Leclerc, Ferrari, Lewis Hamilton, Ferrari, Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing](https://cdn.motorsport.com/images/mgl/01QNOdZ0/s1000/charles-leclerc-ferrari-lewis-.jpg) 
Charles Leclerc, Ferrari, Lewis Hamilton, Ferrari, Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing
Photo by: Steven Tee / LAT Images via Getty Images
Lawson, who replaces the injured Isack Hadjar for the second consecutive weekend, will join Antonelli at the back of the grid with an engine penalty.
Nico Hulkenberg, Carlos Sainz and Esteban Ocon also exited the session at the end of Q2.
In Q1, which was also headed by Gasly ahead of Verstappen and Norris, proved the final station for Racing Bull's replacement driver Yuki Tsunoda, who stood in for Lawson at the New Zealander's regular team.
Tsunoda was on the wrong end of the cut-off in 17th after failing to deliver a clean lap, allowing Williams driver Sainz to escape to Q2 by 0.139s.
Sainz's team-mate Alex Albon also played a role by handing the Spaniard a crucial tow on the straight while the Anglo-Thai driver was down in 18th.
Cadillac defeated Aston Martin at the bottom of the order, with Valtteri Bottas and Sergio Perez comfortably ahead of a struggling Fernando Alonso and Lance Stroll. Alonso didn't complete a final run due to a Honda power unit problem.

title: Newcastle v Bournemouth: How the players rated
author: Ciaran Kelly
content:
![Alex Scott celebrates with Justin Kluivert and Marcus Tavernier](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1024/cpsprodpb/dda3/live/92ab3af0-a927-11f1-b4c6-5d3474716d27.jpg)
Alex Scott has started each of Bournemouth's first three Premier League games this season
- Published
Substitute Jacob Ramsey scored a late equaliser as Newcastle United came from behind to draw 2-2 against Bournemouth at St James' Park.
Here's how I rated the players and you can see how you scored them below.
Newcastle United
Lukas Hornicek: A little unfortunate for the second goal in particular after the ball came back off the upright and bounced off him. One or two moments of miscommunication at the back. 5
Amar Dedic: Made an impressive start to his Newcastle career, and carries a real threat going forward, but caught out defensively for both goals. Did swing in the ball for the equaliser, though. 4
Malick Thiaw: Stand-in captain in Dan Burn's absence once again, but could only watch on as he put through the net after his block on Alex Scott's cross looped into the bottom corner. 5
Sven Botman: A poor clearance before Marcus Tavernier's opener but went on to make a couple of crucial interventions to deny Evanilson. 5
Lewis Hall: Substituted at half-time in the corresponding fixture back in April but coped better with Rayan this time. 6
Nico Gonzalez: Struggled to have the same effect as his impressive debut against Tottenham Hotspur. Missed a tackle on Tavernier before Bournemouth's second goal and only partially blocked Scott's effort in the build-up to the visitors' first. 5
Lewis Miley: So much potential, and still so young at 20, but struggled to get a handle on Bournemouth's midfield. Passing not to usual standard. 5
Anthony Elanga: Quickly frustrated with refereeing decisions going against him. Got little change from Adrien Truffert. 5
Joe Willock: Couldn't fault his effort as he chased down Bournemouth players and attempted to make blocks. Came close to equalising with a header. 5
Harvey Barnes: Stepped up when Newcastle were on very shaky ground with a stunning goal from the hosts' first shot on target. Often frustrated by failure, but always capable of a big moment. 7
Yoane Wissa: Looks better in the number 10 role in this system than up top. Repeatedly dropped deep to get involved. Showed determination to dig out a cross for a big Willock chance. 5
Subs:
Matias Fernandez-Pardo (on 63, Willock): Got a huge welcome on his debut. Quickly won a free-kick and worked hard to win the ball back. 6
Jacob Ramsey: Popped up with a precious equaliser to secure a point with a well-taken finish. 7
Jacob Murphy (on 77, Elanga): 6
Sean Steur (on 77, Gonzalez): 6
Livramento (on 90, Hall)
Subs not used: Nick Pope, Fabian Schar, Aladji Bamba, Bazoumana Toure
Bournemouth
Djordje Petrovic: Little he could do for Barnes' goal, but otherwise a relatively comfortable afternoon. 6
Adam Smith: Played a role in Tavernier's opener by nudging the ball to Scott in the build-up. Tested on one or two moments defensively, but still showing his value at 35. 6
James Hill: Solid. Has already become a very important player for manager Marco Rose. 6
Antonio Silva: Took a nasty blow to the head from Elanga's shoulder, but the summer signing shook it off. 6
Adrien Truffert: Coped expertly with the in-form Elanga and caused Dedic real problems going the other way. 7
Tyler Adams: First competitive start under Rose. Could have got closer to Barnes for Newcastle's goal, but hard to see him coming out of the side after this display. 7
Alex Scott: So influential. Played a key role in both of his side's goals. Passing and vision stood out throughout. 8
Rayan: Not as effective as he was in the corresponding fixture last season. Rose was roaring at him at one stage. 5
Marcus Tavernier: Showed great anticipation to put the visitors in front. He's now scored in each of his past three trips to St James' Park. Could have netted a couple on this visit. 7
Justin Kluivert: Helped set up Bournemouth's crucial second goal after boldly letting fly from 35 yards out. Always a handful. 7
Evanilson: Had a real battle with Botman. Missed a couple of decent chances but worked hard throughout. 6
Subs:
Lewis Cook (on 74, Adams): 6
David Brooks (on 74, Kluivert): 6
Daniel Jebbison (on 89, Tavernier)
Ben Gannon-Doak (on 89, Rayan)
Ryan Christie (on 96, Scott)
Subs not used: Michele Di Gregorio, Julio Soler, Bafode Diakite, Juanlu Sanchez
How did you rate the players?

summary: Newcastle United came from behind to draw 2-2 against Bournemouth at St James' Park, with substitute Jacob Ramsey scoring a late equaliser. Harvey Barnes scored Newcastle's first goal with a stunning effort, while Marcus Tavernier and Alex Scott played key roles in Bournemouth's goals. Alex Scott was named the standout performer for Bournemouth, earning an 8 out of 10 rating.
key_points: Substitute Jacob Ramsey secured a 2-2 draw for Newcastle United with a late equaliser.
Marcus Tavernier scored his third consecutive goal in as many trips to St James' Park for Bournemouth.
Alex Scott was highly influential for Bournemouth, playing a key role in both of their goals and earning the highest player rating of 8.
Harvey Barnes scored Newcastle's first goal with a stunning shot from the hosts' first target attempt.

title: Newcastle United 2-2 Bournemouth: Premier League – live reaction
author: David Tindall
content:
Here’s Jacob Ramsey after his late equaliser rescued a point for Newcastle. “Yeah, to be fair our first three games have been really good. We’re unlucky not to win against Liverpool, a 2-0 against Spurs and a good performance today.
“I thought in the first half we were a little bit slow, didn’t keep the ball well but second half I think we’ve done well. At half-time the manager said that we didn’t win enough duels and I was playing a little bit deeper today so yeah, duels were a big thing.
“I actually thought Bournemouth played really well today, especially in the first half they controlled the game but yeah, thankful to come on and get the goal.
“There was a lot of negativity around Newcastle in pre-season, before the season started and hopefully we can shut them up and we’ve been doing that so far. Don’t want to get too carried away, it’s only our third game but yeah, enjoying it.”
It’s all over and Glenn Hoddle’s 2-2 shout plays out. Bournemouth have now dropped seven points from winning positions in their three matches. Fair play to Newcastle for hanging in there. Barnes’ quick response to make it 2-1 was hugely important and Ramsey kept this cool to strike home one of Newcastle’s rare second-half chances. It’s Newcastle’s second 2-2 home draw of the campaign.
90 min +3: More subs by the way. Gannon-Doak and Jebbison are on for Bournemouth with Rayan and Tavernier going off. For Newcastle, Livramento replaces Hall. More housekeeping as Smith is booked.
Bournemouth concede another late goal and Newcastle are level! Nothing looks to be happening as Murphy’s cross is underhit. But Newcastle recycle the ball, Barnes has a swing and a miss in the box and while others freeze, Ramsey calmly strokes the ball past Petrovic to pull the hosts level.
Jacob Ramsey’s precise finish draws Newcastle level! Photograph: Scott Heppell/Reuters
86 min: When is the late Newcastle charge going to emerge? Nothing so far as Bournemouth continue to press. Marco Rose winning the tactical battle so far.
84 min:Bournemouth take a short free-kick and as the Newcastle wall stands still rather than charges out, Tavernier pings a left-footer which goes well wide. Dozy defending though.
81 min: Boos as Smith slowly limps to the sidelines to get treatment. The camera pans to Dan Burns and his son in the stands. Both smile and Burns Jr give a cheery wave. Has no-one told him the score?! Probably just a lovely, happy fella like his dad.
80 min: The second half has been way less entertaining than the first. Bournemouth have been happy to hold what they have and Newcastle haven’t got their dangerous forwards into the game. All the substitutions have rather affected the flow as well.
79 min: A reminder for Bournemouth that they’ve been leading both their Premier League games so far only to slump to a defeat and a draw from those winning positions.
70 min: Newcastle have scored twice in both their Premier League matches so far. They’ll have to keep that record going to get anything from this. It’s all getting to Jaissle, who is booked for going out of his marked zone.
69 min: Fernandez-Pardo wins a corner and then crosses into the box. Hills heads clear but Bournemouth are somewhat on the back foot now. Some light relief as Scott expertly controls a ball out of the sky before being fouled by Wissa.
67 min: From the free-kick, Hall and Gonzalez combine but the cross is headed clear. It’s hurl into the box time from Dedic but Bournemouth do enough to clear before winning their own free-kick.
summary: Newcastle United secured a 2-2 draw against Bournemouth thanks to a late equalizer from Jacob Ramsey. Bournemouth controlled much of the first half, but Newcastle improved after the break and salvaged a point. The result means Bournemouth have now dropped seven points from winning positions in their opening three matches of the Premier League campaign.
key_points: Jacob Ramsey scored a late goal to rescue a 2-2 draw for Newcastle.
Bournemouth has now dropped seven points from winning positions in their first three matches.
Bournemouth controlled the game in the first half before Newcastle improved after the break.
The match marked Newcastle's second 2-2 home draw of the season.

title: London City Lionesses explained: Michele Kang, Alexia Putellas and the pursuit of Champions League football
author: Anton Toloui
content:
London City Lionesses explained: Michele Kang, Alexia Putellas and the pursuit of Champions League football
Sky Sports News' Anton Toloui answers all the big questions surrounding the WSL's most intriguing newcomers London City Lionesses; watch London City vs Man Utd live on Sky Sports on Friday; kick-off 7pm
Friday 4 September 2026 18:50, UK
London City Lionesses are the Women's Super League's great unknown. A club modest in size, with flashy budgets and ambitions well beyond what would reasonably be considered possible for a side only promoted to the top flight 12 months ago.
Their prospects for the upcoming season are therefore difficult to predict. Billionaire owner Michele Kang has been clear in her intent. She wants Champions League football and has enlisted a group of megastars from across Europe to help her do it.
But such a mission is far from straightforward. It's been 12 years since any side other than Arsenal, Chelsea, Man City and Man Utd finished inside the top three. Since the WSL's inception, in fact, only four clubs have ever won the title.
So, what makes London City Lionesses' bid any different?
- Transfer Centre LIVE! | WSL latest news and transfers
- Got Sky? Watch WSL games LIVE on your phone📱
- Not got Sky? Latest Sky Sports deals or stream WSL games with no contract📺
Counter-culture or genuine contenders?
It would be unfair to reduce a club backed by a corporate giant to a counter-culture. That implies something short-lived. But it's clear Kang wants to disrupt the established order in the WSL.
Similar questions were being asked when Man City entered women's football a decade-and-a-half ago, and now they are a firm fixture of the top three. The latest champions to be crowned.
Kang is trying to repeat the same success, but doing so in 2026 requires a completely different model. Investing in star players is only part of the plan; money is being put into the training ground, youth setup and commercial arms of the club.
The current clubs at the top of the pyramid will be watching to see what works and what doesn't down in Bromley. There is enough reason for the them to pay attention to developments, if not yet show major concern.
Will the money keep flowing?
Initially, investment came directly from Kang's pocket. She insists, however, she is hiring the best commercial brains in the business to increase revenues and make the model sustainable.
London City can spend up to 80 per cent of revenue on their squad, plus another £4m from the hand of their generous owner.
The hope is the buzz around new signings puts bums on seats, but also drives sponsorship opportunities, shirt sales and opens other revenue-enhancing avenues. Alexia Putellas and Mary Earps are names that will push those efforts forward.
Kang is in this for the long-term. She is more than willing to keep investing but is also realistic about needing to see more money come into the club as it continues to grow. And growth will have to be managed differently from others.
London City do not have the luxury of drawing fans from the supporter pool of a men's club, like Arsenal have done so effectively. They are going to have to get creative to entice big crowds.
What does this model mean for the WSL?
That rests largely on how successful London City are this season - and beyond. Chelsea have been the biggest spenders in recent years and won six out of the last seven titles. The maths is quite simple.
Most clubs make operating losses. London's City's latest accounts revealed theirs to be £10.6m in 2024/25. The scale of spending this summer will make for interesting reading when their next set of financials are revealed.
But, if London City go on to have a stellar season, perhaps even win a trophy, then does it not just confirm the old adage of the more you spend the higher the chances are of winning?
Do world-class individuals equal a proper team?
This is the fun bit - who knows how all these big-name stars will come together under one roof? Upon signing, it's clear they have all be united by the female-led approach of Kang. But that does not guarantee a unified team capable of beating the best.
They have signed household names but Earps, Putellas, Mapi Leon, Kadidiatou Diani, Nikita Parris, Danielle van de Donk, Alanna Kennedy, Saki Kumagai, Kosovare Asllani and Elena Linari are all over the age of 30.
No European football means their legs can be well rested but football isn't won with just talent and experience.
The Bromley Glacticos could exhilarate. They might underwhelm. And that is where the proper intrigue lies. Who truly knows?
How does Putellas factor?
It's difficult to downplay the importance of Putellas both on and off the field. She is the current Ballon D'Or favourite and was voted the best player in the Champions League last season.
Teams will naturally target her. Plans will be made to reduce her influence on games. Even if they manage it, though, other star players lie in wait. Just stopping Putellas is not a fail-safe.
The 32-year-old's mentality is almost unmatched, too. You only need a few minutes with her to feel the determination and drive for success. She raises standards simply by being there. Starring in games is a byproduct of that perfectionism.
Plus, she is one of the most commercially popular players on the planet. She changes every single department at a club whose journey is only entering its second term in the top flight.
What about the manager?
Eder Maestre is under the most pressure of anyone at the club.
The club ditched Jocelyn Precheur, a coach with UWCL and French Cup-winning experience, before Christmas last season.
They went for a Spanish coach known for his technical ability and track record of making players better.
The one thing Maestre lacks, though, is experience at a big club. If he doesn't get things moving in the right direction quickly then expect every coach with a stacked medal cabinet to be sending their CVs to Kang for consideration.
Any potholes?
London City have lots of exciting talent. Some approaching the end of their careers, but others just beginning. Those include Freya Godfrey, Lucia Corrales and Isa Kaardinal.
One obvious problem will be balancing the needs of the squad while keeping everyone happy and motivated. Are veteran players going to be content sitting on the bench for weeks at a time?
Every rival wants to beat London City this season to show they are nothing more than an expensive flash in the pan. Winning week-in, week-out against such resistance won't be easy. Teams are intent on putting London City in their place.
Also, this has to work quickly. They do not play any of last season's top three until matchweek eight, which is a favourable start. Maestre has a chance to establish some early rhythm before meeting the big guns. Pressure to perform during such a kind run will be immense.
