title: Premier League transfer talking points: three things we learned from the data
author: Andrew Beasley
content:
Premier League clubs have invested more than £3.4bn in players this summer, an increase of 11.9% on last year. There are three aspects of this enormous spending worthy of closer scrutiny.
Priorities on player age have changed
Premier League clubs are spending less on players in the peak 24-27 age band even though those players are increasingly the core of their selections.
As recently as 2021-22, 40% of minutes were taken by players at least 28 years old at the start of the season. That proportion has dropped each year, reaching 26.6% in 2025-26. The reliance on veterans has declined. The bulk of their lost minutes went to players aged between 24 and 27, which is now the dominant age band.
The spend on that key demographic has fallen by 23% since last summer though. Without Manchester City signing the 25-year-old Enzo Fernández for a British transfer record-equalling £125m shortly before the window closed, the drop would have been even greater.
Younger players account for some of the shortfall but a surprisingly high slice of it has gone towards older footballers. The Premier League has invested £323.3m in players aged at least 28, only around £50m shy of the outlay on this age range in the previous three summers combined (£370.5m). Their proportion of the total has not been as high for four years.
How much this increased spending on veterans affects the playing time figures depends in part on the selection decisions of Mikel Arteta. Arsenal signed two 28-year-olds for a combined £126m: Bruno Guimarães (£75m) and Ezri Konsa (£51m). Transfermarkt considers them to be the most expensive central midfielder and centre-back respectively aged over 27 in history.
The three most expensive Premier League signings of the summer before Fernández – Morgan Rogers, Elliot Anderson and Bradley Barcola – were 23 when their deals were completed. With only slightly less spent collectively on footballers who are 22, clubs have gone hard for players on the verge of entering their peak years rather than those in them.
The Premier League is becoming a closed shop
Perhaps the most notable aspect of transfer spending this summer is how much of it has remained within English football. Fourteen of the 19 signings that cost Premier League clubs at least £50m were made from within the division or from relegated West Ham. Where 30.2% of spending remained in the Premier League in summer 2022, the figure hit 39.3% this year.
after newsletter promotion
With the combined outlay growing by almost £1.5bn in that period, what appears a relatively small percentage shift becomes a significant figure in the accounts. The squad cost ratio rules are unlikely to stem this flow either, because clubs will be happy to sell for inflated fees that can almost only come from within the division.
Barcola was the oldest of the five costliest signings from overseas, with Matias Fernandez-Pardo and Jérémy Jacquet (aged 21), Johan Manzambi (aged 20) and Ayyoub Bouaddi (aged 18) completing the set. The Premier League is able to retain its top stars, its clubs exchanging them among themselves, while having the funds to hoover up the most exciting young talent from elsewhere.
Squad-building trends may be evolving in the Premier League, but the money is here and a significant portion of it is not going anywhere else. English football is starting to become an enclosed ecosystem.
The rest of Europe cannot keep up
Very few clubs across Europe come close to competing financially. The Premier League features a match this weekend between the top two teams in Europe for net spend and it isn’t Arsenal v Chelsea. Liverpool’s trip to Ipswich takes the honour.
The promoted sides have invested enormous sums to try to be competitive. They have all played League One football within the previous eight seasons, yet Real Madrid are the only club from another country with a higher net spend than Hull or Coventry.
The cream of the Premier League crop can probably only move within England. The transfer fee for Rogers (£117m) or Anderson (£116m) was above the net spend of 75 of the 76 top-flight clubs in France, Germany, Italy and Spain. Milan narrowly spent more than the cost of Sandro Tonali (£92.5m) net, but no other side beyond Madrid from mainland Europe did. Most non-English sides would have to have a clearout of talent to raise funds for a single elite player from the Premier League, which isn’t practical.
This financial dominance can be seen in continental competitions. Five English clubs have featured in the past eight Champions League finals, as many teams as the rest of Europe has provided in that time. The Premier League has supplied three of the past four Europa League finalists and three of the past four Conference League winners. This is unlikely to change when relegation favourites in England can outspend all but the very richest clubs overseas.
summary: Premier League clubs increased their summer transfer spending by 11.9% to over £3.4bn, with shifting trends in player ages and a heavy emphasis on trading within England. Clubs spent less on players in the 24-27 peak age band while increasing investments in both younger prospects and surprisingly older veterans. Meanwhile, the financial dominance of English clubs far outstrips the rest of Europe, turning the Premier League into an increasingly enclosed ecosystem.
key_points: Premier League summer transfer spending rose by 11.9% to more than £3.4bn.
Spending on players in the peak 24-27 age band fell by 23%, while investments in players aged 28 and older reached £323.3m.
A significant portion of spending stayed within English football, with 14 of the 19 signings costing at least £50m coming from within the division or relegated West Ham.
Except for Real Madrid and Milan, no top-flight clubs in France, Germany, Italy, and Spain had a net spend exceeding individual multi-million-pound Premier League player transfer fees.

title: Everton & other writings by Paul Quinn, The Analysis Series, Talking the Blues & the esk PodcastsThe Analysis Series: Everton’s 2026 summer transfer window
author: Paul Quinn
content:
|  | 
Summary
The Friedkin Group is running Everton as a recapitalised, cost-disciplined asset to be made compliant and valuable, not resourced to compete. The window is fully consistent with that thesis.
Summary judgements
- Financially rational, sportingly threadbare. Everton committed approximately £74m gross on six permanents (two of them loan conversions), sold Ndiaye for £65m, and ended net-neutral to net-positive, but failed to sign a specialist right-back, a striker, or left-back cover, leaving Moyes with around 18 outfield players and Thierno Barry as the only recognised senior striker after Beto’s sale and the deadline-day collapse of the Folarin Balogun deal.
- The Ndiaye sale settles the ownership question. I previously modelled that a circa-£60m Ndiaye disposal moves Everton’s indicative 2026/27 Squad Cost Ratio from the high 80s to the high 60s, comfortably inside even the 70% UEFA threshold. Combined with reversing the £35m Harrison Armstrong sale on supporter-sentiment grounds, the picture is of an owner optimising a ratio and an asset, not a football team.
- Moyes is exposed; the recruitment function is structurally weak. Moyes, on a reported two-and-a-half-year deal from January 2025, said he needed up to nine or ten players, received a net of three genuine first-team additions, and called it the busiest window of his career.
- Everton has no Director of Football, operating a four-man “Football Leadership Team” under CEO Angus Kinnear: a governance model ill-suited to a regime requiring continuous in-season ratio management.
Key Findings
- Gross spend of approximately £74m (Moyes’s own figure); net spend near break-even to net-positive after deadline-day sales., Everton closed the window broadly net-neutral or net-positive, among the division’s lowest spenders. For context of scale, Deloitte recorded the prior (2025) summer as a record £3.0bn of Premier League gross spend, the window that ended with Liverpool’s £125m signing of Alexander Isak, and Sky Sports’ final tally for summer 2026 put Premier League clubs at a fresh record of £3.48bn.
- The incoming profile was a deliberate reduction in unit cost per squad slot. Six permanents for approximately £74m averages around £12m per slot: Hayden Hackney (£16.5m rising to circa £25m, Middlesbrough), Merlin Röhl (circa £19m, Freiburg, loan made permanent), Tyrique George (£20m-plus, Chelsea, loan made permanent), Christian Nørgaard (circa £7m, Arsenal), Brennan Johnson (straight swap for Dwight McNeil, cash-neutral) and Arthur Barratt (16, Chelsea academy, undisclosed). Ainsley Maitland-Niles (circa £4.2m / €5m, Lyon) was added on deadline day as a compromise right-back. Jack Grealish returned on a season-long loan from Manchester City with no loan fee, Everton paying a reported circa 90% of wages (75% per some outlets) and holding a £50m option.
- Outgoing business was wage-led and, late on, cash-generative. Ndiaye to Manchester City for a confirmed £65m, comprising £60m plus a further £5m in add-ons, on a five-year contract, was the single most consequential transaction. Beto joined Fiorentina (circa £15.4m / €18m), Tim Iroegbunam joined Hull City (reported £13m plus £9m in add-ons) and Nathan Patterson joined Torino (circa £860k / €1m plus a 30% sell-on). Idrissa Gueye (to Al Diriyah), Séamus Coleman and Tyler Onyango left on contract expiry; Adam Aznou went to Málaga on loan.
- Key positions were not addressed. Everton pursued and missed multiple right-backs, Guela Doué (two bids rejected by Strasbourg), Aaron Wan-Bissaka (joined Aston Villa), Daniel Muñoz and Kenny Tete (deal stalled), before settling for Maitland-Niles, who is not a specialist right-back. The Balogun signing (circa £40m from Monaco) collapsed on deadline night over a medical issue and the player’s change of heart; a fallback loan for Joshua Zirkzee was rejected by Manchester United. No striker arrived to replace Beto.
- The Armstrong reversal is the governance signal of the window. Everton reportedly agreed a £35m sale of 19-year-old academy midfielder Harrison Armstrong to Nottingham Forest, then TFG reversed their prior approval following visible supporter opposition, with 1,200 travelling fans singing against the sale at Bournemouth. An academy graduate carries no book value, so £35m would have been pure profit, close to the most SCR-efficient transaction available to the club.
- Financial foundations are transformed. TFG’s restructuring converted Moshiri’s £450.75m loan to equity, injected £233.4m of new equity (later cash injections taking total equity to circa £386m by mid-2026), settled the circa £200m Rights and Media Funding facility and the circa £200m 777/A-CAP exposure, and completed a £350m JP Morgan-led stadium refinancing. Per independent analysis of the FY2024/25 accounts, the recurring wage-to-revenue ratio improved from 83.8% to 77.3% (recurring wage bill down £4.6m to £152.1m against record turnover of £196.7m), and player amortisation near-halved from £64.6m to £50.9m.
Confirmed permanent incomings
| Player | Age | Position | From | Reported fee | Notes | 
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Hayden Hackney | 23 | CM/DM | Middlesbrough | £16.5m rising to c.£25m | Championship Player of the Season 2025/26; PFA Championship Players’ Player of the Year | 
| Merlin Röhl | — | CM | Freiburg | c.£19m | Loan made permanent under pre-agreed obligation; deployed at right-back early season | 
| Tyrique George | — | Winger | Chelsea | £20m+ | Loan made permanent; long-term contract; England youth international | 
| Christian Nørgaard | — | DM | Arsenal | c.£7m | Gueye replacement; joined injured, Moyes pessimistic on return date | 
| Brennan Johnson | 25 | Winger | Crystal Palace | Swap for McNeil | No cash fee disclosed | 
| Arthur Barratt | 16 | Midfield | Chelsea academy | Undisclosed | Long-term development signing | 
| Ainsley Maitland-Niles | 29 | RB/MF | Lyon | c.£4.2m / €5m | Three-year deal plus option; deadline-day right-back compromise | 
Loan in: Jack Grealish (Manchester City, season-long, no loan fee, circa 90% of wages reported, 75% per some outlets, with a £50m option to buy).
Confirmed outgoings
| Player | To | Basis | Reported terms | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Iliman Ndiaye | Manchester City | Permanent | £65m confirmed (£60m + £5m add-ons); five-year deal | 
| Beto | Fiorentina | Permanent | c.£15.4m / €18m (club: undisclosed) | 
| Tim Iroegbunam | Hull City | Permanent | c.£13m + £9m add-ons (club: undisclosed); bought from Villa c.£9m in 2024 | 
| Nathan Patterson | Torino | Permanent | c.£860k / €1m + 30% sell-on; cost c.£12m from Rangers in 2022 | 
| Dwight McNeil | Crystal Palace | Swap | Swap for Johnson; no cash | 
| Idrissa Gueye | Al Diriyah | Contract expiry | Free; senior wage removed | 
| Séamus Coleman | Released | Contract expiry | Free; long-serving captain | 
| Tyler Onyango | Released | Contract expiry | Marginal | 
| Adam Aznou | Málaga | Loan | Left-back sent out for game time | 
Pursued and not completed
Folarin Balogun (Monaco, circa £40m, collapsed on deadline day over a medical issue and the player’s change of heart);
Joshua Zirkzee (Manchester United, circa £10m loan package rejected);
Kenny Tete (Fulham, deal stalled);
Guela Doué (Strasbourg, two bids rejected);
Aaron Wan-Bissaka (joined Aston Villa);
Daniel Muñoz (Crystal Palace);
Jonathan Rowe (Bologna, circa £30m bid rejected);
Richarlison (Tottenham, circa £35m return discussed, did not proceed);
Djed Spence; Kyle Walker (disputed); Zian Flemming (cooled).
Net spend and accounting treatment
Everton’s approximately £74m gross committed outlay comprises modest cash fees (Hackney, Röhl, George, Nørgaard, Maitland-Niles), a cash-neutral swap (Johnson for McNeil) and an undisclosed academy fee (Barratt). Against that, deadline-day sales generated roughly £93m-plus of gross receipts, Ndiaye £65m, Beto circa £15.4m, Iroegbunam circa £13m initial, Patterson circa £0.85m, pushing the window to net-neutral or net-positive.
On the five-year measure from 2022/23, Everton’s cumulative net spend of circa €94m ranks among the division’s lowest, consistent with the club’s status as one of the Premier League’s most restrained net spenders.
From PSR to Squad Cost Ratio
SCR is squad costs, player and head-coach wages, plus player-registration amortisation and impairment, plus agents’ fees, divided by adjusted revenue. The Green Threshold is 85% for non-UEFA clubs and 70% for UEFA clubs; the Red Threshold is 115%. Everton did not qualify for Europe and therefore face the 85% threshold.
| Under PSR, the profit on an academy or homegrown sale, sale price less residual book value, fell straight into the loss calculation, making such sales the most efficient compliance instrument available. Under SCR, that profit only dilutes into the denominator, while removing a high-wage, high-amortisation player from the numerator now delivers the greater benefit.Everton’s wage-led outgoing business, Gueye and Coleman on expiry, McNeil by swap, is precisely rational under this logic. | 
Indicative SCR modelling
My own indicative modelling, built on the last audited cost base and expressly not a forecast, placed Everton’s 2026/27 numerator at circa £207m against a denominator of circa £245m, giving a no-material-sale SCR in the high 80s, above the Green Threshold and consuming multi-year allowance in year one. That modelling held that a disposal at circa £60m against a low residual book value moves the indicative ratio from the high 80s to the high 60s, comfortably inside even the 70% UEFA threshold.
Everton took that sale, at £65m. On the model’s assumptions, that moves the club comfortably inside even the UEFA threshold and preserves its full multi-year allowance.
The audited position
| FY2024/25 (year to 30 June 2025) | Figure | Movement | 
|---|---|---|
| Turnover | £196.7m | Record | 
| Total club wages | £152.1m | Down £4.6m (recurring) | 
| Wage-to-revenue (recurring) | 77.3% | Improved from 83.8% | 
| Player amortisation | £50.9m | Down from £64.6m | 
| Profit on player trading | £31.3m | — | 
| Headline pre-tax loss | £8.6m | From £53.2m | 
| Underlying pre-tax loss | c.£57.8m | Excluding £49.2m intragroup gain | 
The headline loss is flattered by a £49.2m intragroup gain on the sale of the women’s team and Goodison Park Stadium Ltd to parent Roundhouse Capital. That gain is worth nothing under SCR, which excludes asset-disposal gains, or under UEFA rules.
The Armstrong non-sale forfeited circa £35m of pure profit that would have been an unqualified addition to the SCR denominator. Its reversal establishes that this ownership will subordinate ratio optimisation to supporter sentiment in identifiable cases.
Squad assessment, stronger or weaker?
|  | 
Position by position
- Striker; weakened. Beto sold; Balogun collapsed; Zirkzee rejected. Thierno Barry (23) is the sole recognised senior number nine, supported by the converted winger Tyrique George. A strikeforce that scored only 18 goals in 2025/26, within a team total of 47 league goals, joint sixth-lowest, lost significant output. Ndiaye (the club’s top scorer), Beto and Gueye together represented 17 goals leaving the club.
- Right-back; not solved. The specialist right-back Moyes sought publicly for over a year did not arrive. Maitland-Niles (a midfielder by origin) and Röhl (a central midfielder) have been used there. Patterson and Coleman both left.
- Left-back; weakened. Aznou loaned out, leaving Vitaliy Mykolenko with no specialist backup.
- Central midfield; strengthened. Hackney (Championship Player of the Season) plus Nørgaard (though he joined injured), alongside Röhl, James Garner, Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall, Charly Alcaraz and the retained Armstrong.
- Wide and attacking areas; mixed. Johnson adds directness and pace; George adds carrying threat. Grealish’s loan is a genuine quality addition but is a wide creator, not a fix for the striker or full-back gaps.
- Age profile and resale; improved. The English-qualified sub-24 profile (Johnson, Hackney, George, Barratt, Armstrong) builds homegrown compliance and appreciating assets, asset warehousing consistent with the ownership model. Core assets Jarrad Branthwaite (circa €45m, contract to 2030) and Jordan Pickford (circa €14m, to 2029) were retained.
The gap between the squad Moyes asked for and the squad he received is the defining sporting fact of the window.
The Friedkin ownership thesis
| The evidence firmly supports the proposition that The Friedkin Group is prioritising financial robustness and non-reliance on shareholder funding over on-pitch success. Every material decision since December 2024 has reduced Everton’s cost of running or increased its asset value. Almost none has increased short-term competitive capacity. | 
Capital and debt
Moshiri’s £450.75m shareholder loan was converted to equity, with a capital reduction cleansing accumulated losses. £233.4m of new equity was injected at £174.66 per share. The circa 10%-plus Rights and Media Funding facility and the circa £200m 777/A-CAP exposure were settled, and a £350m JP Morgan-led refinancing, reported oversubscribed, completed in March 2025. Cumulative equity injections reached circa £386m by mid-2026, with a further £38m share issue (221,954 shares at £175) in July 2026 to fund the Burnley compensation award, and a £13.8m issue (79,000 shares at £175) dated 27 July 2026 to bolster the transfer kitty.
Stadium and commercial
Hill Dickinson Stadium (52,888 capacity, circa £750–800m cost) opened in August 2025, lifting average league attendance to circa 52,132 from circa 39,000 and delivering a widely estimated circa £40m annual revenue uplift. Naming rights are worth circa £10m a year; the Castore kit deal circa £20m (against circa £8m previously); and CMC Markets front-of-shirt plus Stake sleeve circa £25m combined for 2026/27.
Contingent liabilities
The Burnley commission of 10 June 2026 ordered £26m in damages plus £9.1m interest, with further interest potentially taking the total close to £40m, against Burnley’s original £51.7m claim. Everton are appealing, describing the ruling as fundamentally flawed in both law and fact. The Leeds claim was settled on undisclosed terms; Leicester, Forest and Southampton did not proceed.
Public framing
CEO Angus Kinnear defined the objective as banishing the triple threats of financial instability, relegation risk and regulatory sanction, three defensive axes, none of them competitive. He described the budget as hoping for the maximum spend of what the club is allowed to spend.
The Roma control case
In the same window Roma spent heavily: a reported net spend of roughly €113m (expenditure circa €160.85m against income circa €47.5m), signing Malen permanently plus Santiago Castro, Koulierakis, Mora, Molina and others, on a reported circa €100m budget after returning to the Champions League.
This cuts against a naive “TFG never spends” reading, and reinforces the underlying model. TFG will invest where a club has qualified for the Champions League and has a UEFA settlement to service, that is, where investment protects and compounds enterprise value.
Everton, mid-table and non-European, does not clear that bar. TFG has also deliberately avoided intragroup Roma–Everton transfers: Pursuit Sports, launched 16 July 2025, is framed as centralised back-office and data provision, not a player pipeline, which is both a reputational and a regulatory choice.
Counter-arguments, weighed
The circa £386m of equity and the July cash injections are real commitments, and TFG could inject more and remain SCR-compliant. The honest conclusion is nonetheless firm: TFG has made Everton safe and valuable; it has not, on this window’s evidence, resourced Everton to challenge.
David Moyes’s Position
Moyes returned in January 2025 on a reported two-and-a-half-year contract. During the window he stated he needed quite a few players, having earlier indicated a requirement for up to nine or ten, and called it the busiest window of his career. After the United States tour he said that, having signed three, Everton were still in need of maybe five or six players.
He also put the spend at circa £74m and adopted standard vendor language on Ndiaye, that the club were certainly not in a hurry to sell their best players, a posture the club then contradicted by selling him for £65m.
- Contractual: secure into 2027.
- Tactical: handed a squad with a striker vacuum, no specialist right-back and no left-back cover.
- Political: he has protected himself by publicly and repeatedly stating the squad is unfinished, ensuring accountability for the shortfall attaches to recruitment and ownership rather than to him. His remark that supporters aren’t always wrong, on the Armstrong reversal, aligned him with the fanbase against the board.
Early season and projection
Results have flattered the underlying position: a 2–0 opening win over Crystal Palace (Dewsbury-Hall and Barry, Everton’s first opening-day win in five years, with Pickford decisive), a 1–1 draw at Bournemouth rescued by a Tarkowski equaliser in the 91st minute, and a 4–0 Carabao Cup win at Preston. The Bournemouth performance, trailing 1–0 into stoppage time, illustrates the thin margins.
With 47 league goals last season and the attack weakened, a realistic projection is another lower-half, thirteenth-type finish absent a strong January. The risk to Moyes rises sharply if injuries expose the lack of depth. Ownership’s inaction at his priority positions signals that his sporting requests are subordinate to the ratio, a misalignment that becomes acute if results slide.
Recruitment function and executive assessment
Everton abolished the Director of Football role in favour of a four-man Football Leadership Team: Nick Cox (technical director), James Smith (director of scouting and recruitment), Chris Howarth (football strategy and analytics, with TFG acquiring his Insight Sport consultancy) and Nick Hammond (head of player trading), the last a former Reading DoF, West Brom technical director and Celtic head of football operations who previously consulted for Kinnear at Leeds. The manager works directly with the CEO and ownership.
| The SCR regime requires continuous, in-season management of a single ratio,  a compliance test on 1 March, with SSR liquidity and equity tests each 7 July. That demands a single accountable owner of the squad-cost line who can trade against it in real time. A CEO has a broader remit; a manager has a structural interest in a larger squad. Kinnear’s “maximum spend of what we are allowed” framing is a budget-consumption posture, not a ratio-management one. | 
Outcomes: mixed to poor
The 2025/26 class; circa £111m gross: Dibling up to £42m, Dewsbury-Hall £25m, Barry £27m, Aznou £8m, delivered few hits. Dewsbury-Hall and the Grealish loan were successes; Dibling, Barry, Aznou and Röhl underwhelmed initially.
On selling, Everton negotiated well: Ndiaye at £65m from a £15m purchase, Iroegbunam at circa £13m-plus from circa £9m. On buying at need, the function failed, repeated right-back misses over a year, a striker vacuum, and a chaotic deadline day that left everything late. Against peer benchmarks (Brighton, Brentford, Bournemouth, Crystal Palace, Nottingham Forest), all of whom have built repeatable value-creation models, Everton’s process looks reactive and, in the phrase used by supporters, scattergun.
On the CEO
Kinnear’s career record, Arsenal commercial director at the Emirates move, West Ham managing director at the Olympic Stadium, eight years as Leeds CEO through promotion, relegation and re-promotion, is strong on stadium transition and commercial delivery, precisely the phase Everton is in.
But the recruitment structure he has overseen since arriving at Everton has not yet demonstrated value creation on the buy side.
Summary
Accountability for the sporting shortfall of this window sits squarely with the executive and ownership, not the manager.
In summary, despite our status as ever present members of the Premier League, and despite the significant reconstruction of Everton’s finances we are
- (i) Nowhere near being competitive at the top end of the Premier League financially
- (ii) We cannot retain talent that wishes to perform at the highest levels (Champions League,
- (iii) Cannot attract talent with those aspirations,
- (iv) We do not have a recruitment structure that can meet even the limited expectations of our manager.
- (v) Perhaps most dammingly, have an ownership that does not share the higher ambitions of our fan base, does not seek competitive improvement but seeks cost reduction and a shareholder-centric view of creating value whilst minimising future capital commitments
The Friedkins must publish their competitive objective.
The gap between banishing the triple threats and supporter expectation is untenable and for them a reputational liability. TFG must state whether 2026/27 is explicitly a foundational/consolidation year, or consistent with their future running of the club.
Practically they must re-examine their recruitment methodology. In my opinion they must appoint a single accountable sporting executive who owns the squad-cost line. The four-man committee is unsuited to continuous ratio management. A Director of Football, or a clearly empowered Hammond, with explicit authority over in-season trading against the 1 March test should be installed before the January window.
As an act of good faith and future intent, ring-fence the Ndiaye proceeds for January and treat the striker vacancy as a first-order risk. The single highest-leverage action is to convert the SCR headroom the Ndiaye sale created into a genuine number nine in January.
Evertonians are used to disappointment, we are used to being underwhelmed, we are used to owners not having the ambition, talent or resources to match our expectations of our wonderful, amazing club. The Friedkins still have an opportunity to turn that 50 year cycle around. Communication in the very first instance, followed by a very clear plan on how we regain our competitive position, how we become a trophy winning club, worthy of our fan base and our wonderful city, a city that despite the above can still boast Everton as the senior club in the city.
summary: During the 2026 summer transfer window, The Friedkin Group operated Everton as a cost-disciplined asset focused on financial compliance rather than squad depth. The club committed approximately £74 million gross on six permanent signings while generating significant funds through late sales, notably Iliman Ndiaye to Manchester City for £65 million. Consequently, manager Sean Moyes was left with a threadbare squad that failed to address critical gaps at striker, right-back, and left-back cover.
key_points: Everton committed roughly £74 million gross across six permanent signings while ending the window net-neutral or net-positive due to late sales.
The high-profile £65 million sale of Iliman Ndiaye successfully lowered Everton's indicative Squad Cost Ratio into compliance ranges.
Key squad positions were left unaddressed after pursuits for a specialist right-back and striker Folarin Balogun failed.
The proposed £35 million sale of academy player Harrison Armstrong was reversed following intense supporter opposition, forfeiting pure profit.
Financial restructurings by the owners transformed the club's foundations, improving the recurring wage-to-revenue ratio and reducing player amortisation.

title: Tiger Woods handed five-year driving ban after no-contest plea over crash
author: Guardian sport
content:
Tiger Woods pleaded no contest to reckless driving on Wednesday morning as part of an agreement with Florida prosecutors that reduced a DUI charge stemming from his rollover crash in March.
The 50-year-old was adjudicated guilty of willful and wanton reckless driving, a second offense, during a hearing in Martin County court. Under the agreement, Woods was fined $1,000 and had his driver’s license suspended for five years. Prosecutors had originally charged him with driving under the influence with property damage.
Woods also pleaded no contest to refusing to submit to a lawful test and was fined $500 on that count. He received a concurrent five-year license suspension on a careless-driving citation and agreed not to seek a hardship exemption during the suspension. Court records show he paid $2,131.44 in fines and costs following Wednesday’s hearing.
The plea agreement brings an end to the criminal case arising from the golfer’s crash near his Florida home on Jupiter Island. He had previously pleaded not guilty to both charges.
Woods, dressed in a dark suit and tie, arrived at the Martin County Courthouse seated in the front passenger seat of a black SUV. He did not answer questions from the gathered reporters as he and his girlfriend, Vanessa Trump, walked in and out of the building for the change of plea hearing.
The charges stemmed from a 27 March crash in Hobe Sound. Martin County sheriff John Budensiek said Woods was driving a Land Rover that overturned after he attempted to overtake a truck on a narrow two-lane road shortly before 2pm.
The truck had been slowing to turn into a driveway when Woods approached at what Budensiek described as a “high rate of speed” on a road with a 30mph limit. Woods’s vehicle clipped a trailer, veered off and came to rest on its driver’s side after sliding along the roadway.
Woods, who was alone in the vehicle, was able to exit through the passenger side and was not injured. Investigators said he showed signs of impairment and subjected him to roadside tests before taking him into custody.
A breath test showed no alcohol in his system, but Woods refused to provide a urine sample for drug testing. He told investigators he had taken several medications earlier that day, including drugs for high blood pressure and cholesterol as well as ibuprofen and the prescription painkiller Vicodin, according to court filings released by prosecutors.
The filings also detailed a series of unusual remarks Woods made to officers at the scene. About an hour after the crash, he spoke of “10 to 15 drones” equipped with GoPro cameras flying over his home and car. At another point, after stepping away while on the phone, Woods told an officer he had “just [been] talking to the president” before trailing off. The documents did not identify which president he meant, although Donald Trump said later that day that he had spoken with Woods following the crash.
Woods also told officers he had been looking down at his phone to change the radio station when the collision occurred.
Prosecutors later sought access to Woods’s prescription records from the months leading up to the crash. His attorneys objected, arguing that the records were private, and asked a judge to determine whether they were relevant to the case and to restrict their disclosure.
Days after his arrest, Woods announced that he would step away from golf “to seek treatment and focus on my health”. A judge subsequently granted him permission to travel abroad to enter an inpatient treatment facility, which his attorney said was necessary for an intensive, individualized program.
The crash marked another high-profile traffic incident for Woods. In February 2021, he was seriously injured when his SUV veered off a road in Los Angeles at high speed, leaving him with leg and ankle injuries so severe that doctors considered amputation.
He was also arrested on a DUI charge in south Florida in 2017 after police found him asleep behind the wheel of a damaged vehicle. Woods later said he had taken a problematic combination of prescription medications and pleaded guilty to reckless driving.
Another incident took place in 2009, when Woods crashed his SUV into a fire hydrant and a tree outside his home in Windermere, Florida.
Woods has played a limited schedule in recent years amid chronic pain, injuries and multiple surgeries, including a seventh back procedure and a ruptured achilles tendon. He has not competed in an official PGA Tour event since July 2024.
An 82-time winner on the PGA Tour, Woods is tied with Sam Snead for the most victories in tour history. The 15-time major champion last won one at the 2019 Masters, his fifth title at Augusta National.
summary: Tiger Woods pleaded no contest to reckless driving and refusing a lawful test in a Martin County court, resolving a criminal case stemming from his March rollover crash near his Florida home. Under the agreement, he received a five-year driver's license suspension, a $1,000 fine for reckless driving, and a $500 fine for refusing the test. The charges originated from an incident where Woods's vehicle overturned after attempting to overtake a truck at a high speed, leading investigators to note signs of impairment and prescription medications in his system.
key_points: Tiger Woods pleaded no contest to willful and wanton reckless driving and refusing to submit to a lawful test.
He received a five-year driver's license suspension and agreed not to seek a hardship exemption.
The charges stemmed from a March rollover crash in Hobe Sound after his vehicle clipped a trailer while attempting to overtake a truck.
Woods told investigators he had taken several medications that day, including Vicodin, and showed signs of impairment.
Following the arrest, Woods announced he would step away from golf to seek inpatient treatment for his health.

title: Every Premier League club’s transfer window ranked
author: Mike McGrath
content:
For the second summer in succession, Premier League clubs spent more than £3bn in the transfer market with four players surpassing the £100m barrier.
Enzo Fernández secured a deadline-day move from Chelsea to Manchester City to match the record Premier League transfer fee of £125m, but all 20 clubs made deals which illustrated that England possesses the most lucrative league in the world. Below is our ranking, from worst to best, of each team according to their summer transfer business.
Scroll down or click here to vote on which club had the best window.
summary: Premier League clubs spent over £3bn in the transfer market for the second consecutive summer, with four players exceeding the £100m mark. Enzo Fernández's deadline-day move from Chelsea to Manchester City equaled the record Premier League transfer fee of £125m. The activity highlights the financial dominance of the English league, leading to a comprehensive ranking of all 20 clubs' summer business.
key_points: Premier League clubs spent a total of over £3bn during the summer transfer window.
Four players transferred for fees exceeding £100m.
Enzo Fernández moved from Chelsea to Manchester City for a record-tying £125m fee.
All 20 Premier League clubs completed deals that underscored the league's immense financial power.

title: Arthur Fery sunk by Lorenzo Musetti in straight sets on US Open debut
author: Tumaini Carayol
content:
Six weeks on from the fortnight that changed his life, Arthur Fery’s first grand slam appearance since his semi-final run at Wimbledon came under considerably different circumstances. He is now the 33rd best men’s player in the world, a direct entrant for all of the biggest tournaments, and he has continued to gain experience at the highest level of professional tennis each week.
As a result of his continued exposure on the tour, though, Fery’s adversaries have also learned a bit more about him. In his first main draw appearance at the US Open, Fery came up against a prepared and sharp Lorenzo Musetti, who knew exactly how to exploit the vulnerable parts of his game in order to secure a win. The Italian comprehensively outplayed the British No 1, reaching the second round with a comfortable 6-3, 6-3, 7-5 victory.
This was an emphatic, impressive performance from Musetti, who handcuffed Fery with his heavy topspin and simply had far too many options for his opponent. Despite fighting hard until the end, Fery’s game looked underpowered as he struggled to consistently hit through one of the best defensive players in the world.
Fery had actually started well enough, quickly finding rhythm behind his serve as he eased through his first three service games. However, as the Italian began to take control of the baseline with his forehand, the Briton’s serve capitulated. Down 15-30 at 3-3, Fery threw in his first two double faults of the match on consecutive points to hand over the first break.
Once that was secured, Musetti opened up his shoulders and imposed relentless pressure on Fery. Musetti spent much of the match pushing Fery behind the baseline with his heavy spin and height. With the ball consistently bouncing high above his shoulders and out of his strike zone, Fery struggled to counter Musetti effectively. He veered between desperately trying to take the ball on the rise, constantly spraying errors, and being dictated to by Musetti whenever he tried to hang back and wait for the ball to drop. He never really looked comfortable.
Over the course of their two hours on court, Musetti also made use of his far greater weaponry. He served well in decisive moments and effortlessly stepped inside the baseline, dominating with his forehand when necessary.
He also struck his sweet single-handed backhand supremely well on certain key points, particularly in the second set, where he converted the decisive break point and then saved a later break point with supreme down-the-line backhand winners.
In the aftermath of his shock run to the Wimbledon semi-finals, Fery has managed himself well. He performed at a high level in Cincinnati, winning a round and then pushing Alex de Minaur, the world No 8, in two tight sets. Last week, he reached his first ATP final in Winston-Salem, providing more evidence that he belongs at this level.
![Elena Rybakina in action against Thea Frodin](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/aaa596bc9663806b59b3e5440913e6838121e55d/0_0_4650_2902/master/4650.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
He is yet to lose to any lower-ranked opponent. But the standard at the top of men’s tennis is incredibly high and competing with players of Musetti’s calibre will come with many more losses and lessons. It remains to be seen how much these lessons will enable him to improve.
For Musetti, this is a hopeful first performance as he tries to put himself back in contention for big titles after a torrid year. Musetti had started the season ranked No 5 and he was en route to a first Australian Open semi-final in Melbourne when he was forced to withdraw due to injury while leading Novak Djokovic by two sets in their quarter-final match. After a few months out, it has taken even longer for Musetti to rebuild confidence in his game and body. He is finally beginning to resemble his old self again.
Elsewhere, Elena Rybakina made a positive step forward in her pursuit of the No 1 ranking as she moved into the second round with a 6-3, 6-2 win over the 17-year-old American wildcard Thea Frodin.
![Flavio Cobolli screams in delights](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/5b1b04ec315518a95a55c3187a684b52e6923b80/0_0_2287_1536/master/2287.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
There have been ample doubts surrounding Rybakina after she suffered a foot injury at the Cincinnati Open that forced her to retire from her quarter-final match against Iga Swiatek but she appeared comfortable on the court as she overpowered her inexperienced opponent.
Rybakina currently sits at No 1 in the live rankings and she would become the world No 1 for the first time in her career if she reaches the semi-finals or if Aryna Sabalenka, Jessica Pegula and Coco Gauff do not win the tournament.
In the men’s draw, the fifth seed and French Open finalist Flavio Cobolli produced one of the best comebacks of his career to escape a tough battle with the Argentinian Francisco Comesaña, recovering from a two-set deficit to reach the second round with a 3-6, 2-6, 6-3, 6-4, 6-4 win.
summary: British No 1 Arthur Fery suffered a straight-sets defeat to Lorenzo Musetti on his US Open main draw debut. Musetti utilized heavy topspin and a dominant forehand to overcome Fery 6-3, 6-3, 7-5. Elsewhere in the tournament, Elena Rybakina advanced to the second round with a straight-sets win, and Flavio Cobolli completed a remarkable comeback from two sets down against Francisco Comesaña.
key_points: Lorenzo Musetti defeated Arthur Fery 6-3, 6-3, 7-5 in the first round of the US Open.
Fery struggled to handle Musetti's heavy topspin and high-bouncing shots throughout the match.
Elena Rybakina defeated 17-year-old wildcard Thea Frodin 6-3, 6-2 to move into the second round.
Flavio Cobolli overcame a two-set deficit to beat Francisco Comesaña in a five-set thriller.

title: Chelsea transfer news: Lamine Camara's Â£47.1m move from Monaco collapses
author: Nizaar Kinsella
content:
![Lamine Camara pinches his shirt](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/962/cpsprodpb/f8ad/live/9704b0d0-a644-11f1-9547-7578d73af9f6.jpg)
Lamine Camara has won 37 caps for Senegal
- Published
Lamine Camara will be staying at Monaco after the Senegal midfielder's Â£47.1m move to Chelsea collapsed.
The 22-year-old had already completed a medical with Chelsea but his switch fell through shortly after the 23:00 BST deadline.
They had two bids rejected by the Ligue 1 side before Monaco eventually lowered their asking price when Folarin Balogun's move to Everton came into renewed doubt.
Chelsea made their move for Camara in an attempt to bolster midfield options with Enzo Fernandez closing in on a joint-British transfer record Â£125m switch to Manchester City.
They had also held talks with Roma's Manu Kone and another unnamed Premier League option.
One of the club's aims this summer was to emerge from the transfer window with a stronger squad despite selling Fernandez to a direct rival.
Chelsea believe they have achieved that after signing Morgan Rogers from Aston Villa in a club-record Â£117m deal, centre-back Maxence Lacroix from Crystal Palace and, most recently, goalkeeper Emiliano Martinez from Aston Villa.
The club have also recruited strikers Emmanuel Emegha and Danny Welbeck, winger Geovany Quenda, midfielders Jordan Henderson and Valentin Barco, as well as full-backs Marco Palestra and Pep Chavarria.
Alonso's side have won all three of their matches this season, beating Fulham and Brighton in the Premier League, and have also reached the third round of the Carabao Cup with victory over Luton Town.
summary: Lamine Camara's £47.1m transfer from Monaco to Chelsea collapsed shortly after the deadline, despite the midfielder having completed a medical. Chelsea pursued Camara to bolster their midfield as Enzo Fernandez neared a £125m move to Manchester City. Despite the failed deal, Chelsea strengthened their squad this summer through several other notable signings, including Morgan Rogers, Maxence Lacroix, and Emiliano Martinez.
key_points: Lamine Camara's £47.1m move to Chelsea collapsed after the deadline following a completed medical.
Monaco lowered their asking price earlier in negotiations when Folarin Balogun's move to Everton faced renewed doubt.
Chelsea targeted Camara as Enzo Fernandez approached a £125m transfer to Manchester City.
Chelsea's summer additions include club-record signing Morgan Rogers, Maxence Lacroix, and Emiliano Martinez.
Alonso's side has won all three of its matches this season across the Premier League and Carabao Cup.

title: Football transfer deadline day: Manchester City sign Ndiaye and agree £125m Fernández deal – live
author: Will Unwin; Daniel Harris; Luke McLaughlin; Daniel Gallan; Jacob Steinberg; Andy Hunter; Jamie Jackson; Niall McVeigh; Louise Taylor; Ed Aarons; Ben Fisher; Andrew Beasley; Barry Glendenning; Marcela Mora y Araujo; David Hytner; Suzanne Wrack; Billy Munday; Nick Ames
content:
Manchester City agree £125m deal to sign Fernández
Jacob Steinberg
Manchester City have agreed a £125m deal to sign Enzo Fernández from Chelsea, equalling the British transfer record. It is a fixed fee with no add-ons or performance-related clauses.
The Argentina international Enzo Fernández, formerly of Benfica and River Plate, will join Manchester City for a £125m fee. Photograph: Dennis Goodwin/ProSports/Shutterstock
Manchester City have completed the signing of Iliman Nidaye for a fee that could rise to £65m. The Senegal international had three years remaining on his Everton contract and had scored 17 goals in 74 appearances for the club.
David Moyes said just over a week ago that it would take “an absolutely outrageous bid” for Everton to sell their prized asset yet the club’s hierarchy, conscious of squad ratio cost pressures, have let him go for less than what City sold Savinho for.
With Beto gone and doubts emerging over Folarin Balogun’s medical results, Ndiaye’s exit could leave Everton in a very precarious position.
Manchester City have confirmed the signing of Iliman Ndiaye from Everton for £60m plus £5m, the 26-year-old signing a five-year contract.
The wide forward said: “City are one of the best clubs in the world and I’ve seen them win everything as I’ve grown up. To be able to write my own chapter in a story that special is the chance of a lifetime and I’m determined to grab it with both hands. It’s not always been easy in my career, but I always had the belief that I could play for a team challenging for the biggest prizes and now I’m here. It feels so good. I love to play with the ball on the floor in an attacking team that wants to score as many goals as possible. That’s why I know this is the perfect fit.”
Ndiaye was loaned from Sheffield United, his first club, to Hyde United for the second half of the 2019-20 season and has also played for Marseille.
Thanks Niall. Phew, things are hotting up. Especially in the two-club race to sign Malik Fofana.
As Louise Taylor says:
Sunderland’s owner, Kyril Louis-Dreyfus has flown to Lyon to try to persuade Malick Fofana to join Lyon rather than Crystal Palace and there is a sense Sunderland have won the race for his signature after the winger underwent a medical in France commissioned by both the north east club and Crystal Palace.
Sunderland, meanwhile, are hoping to sign a second winger in Benfica’s Dodi Lukebakio before the deadline.
A big deal is now officially done: Manchester City have signed Everton forward Iliman Ndiaye in a transfer worth a reported £65m in total – £60m up front and £5m in add-ons.
“Manchester City is delighted to announce the signing of Iliman Ndiaye from Everton,” an official statement said. “The 26-year-old forward has signed a five-year contract, keeping him at the Etihad Stadium until the summer of 2031.”
Manchester United made a late enquiry to Manchester City for their left-back Rayan Aït-Nouri, but the 25-year-old will not be leaving. This seems a little late, and a scattergun approach from United.
“Why does Malick Fofana need to come to England at all tonight?” asks Iain Chambers. “Can’t he just sign a contract of whichever club he eventually chooses, pop home for a kip, and make an early morning start on packing up his PlayStation & some autumn clothing choices?”
Yes, it’s one of those old-fashioned curiosities of the transfer deadline that players must be whisked off to sign the paperwork in an empty stadium, when the whole thing could have been a Zoom call.
More on Malick Fofana’s plane dilemma – Ed Aarons reports that “Palace manager Pierre Sage has also spoken to the 21-year-old on the phone again this evening, having made contact earlier on today. The pair previously worked together at Lyon.” Presumably, Sage talked up Croydon’s excellent transport links with Gatwick and central London.
Any Arsenal fans awaiting transfer updates: how about an entire baseball team? Stan Kroenke, owner of the Premier League champions and the NFL’s LA Rams, is poised to buy the MLB’s Los Angeles Angels, who are based in Anaheim.
There’s a striker merry-go-round on the continent; with Nick Woltemade joining Juve on loan, Jonathan David has left Turin for Madrid, signing for Atlético on an initial loan. Júlian Alvarez, meanwhile, is still an Atleti player with the clock running down.
Everton’s pursuit of Folarin Balogun has left Beto surplus to requirements, so he’s off to Fiorentina for €18m – with former Everton forward Moise Kean joining Como on loan. Another man leaving Florence is Albert Gudmundsson, who moves to Lazio, freeing up Boulaye Dia to join Ligue 1’s Rennes on loan. Keeping up with all that? Good.
“The Malick Fofana tarmac tension is really something else. Let’s face it, it might come down to which of the two planes is nicer,” writes Peter Oh. Sky are reporting that Sunderland chairman Kyril Louis-Dreyfus is on the ground in Lyon, trying to persuade Fofana to choose his side. Palace need to bring out the big guns – Ikea, Boxpark etc.
Patterson also becomes, by my reckoning, the eighth Scottish player currently on the books of a Serie A club – and joins international teammate Ché Adams at Torino.
The transfer window has closed in France, Germany and Italy – it’s open until midnight in Spain – and one headline late move sees keeper Robert Sánchez leaving Chelsea and joining Como on loan, following Emi Martínez’s move to Stamford Bridge.
Nathan Patterson has completed his permanent move from Everton to Torino, becoming the second player from the club to move to Italy on deadline day after Beto. Everton will receive a modest sum for the Scotland international, plus a sell-on fee. The 24-year-old joined the club for £12m from Rangers in 2022 but struggled with injuries and to secure a regular starting role under a series of managers.
Kevin Danso has joined Sunderland on a year-long loan from Tottenham that should lead to a formal £25m transfer for the Austria centre-half next summer.
Meanwhile in the day’s maddest transfer, Lyon’s Malick Fofana has undergone a medical in France jointly commissioned by Sunderland and Crystal Palace as their tug of war to sign him continues.
Two private jets still wait at Lyon airport, waiting to transport him to either south London or the north east.
West Ham’s financial demands for Edson Alvarez expected to see the Mexican midfielder stay.
He is not in squad to face Wolves [tonight in the Championship]. Nor is Magassa. Club want to keep him. Have had bids but none met valuation. Meanwhile ownership hopeful Amanda Staveley is here as the battle for control for the club edges towards a conclusion.
Crystal Palace look set for another frantic end to deadline day as they await Malick Fofana’s decision over whether to pick them over Sunderland.
The Belgium forward is still said to be weighing up his decision, although Palace have lined Darío Osorio from Danish side Midtjylland if that falls through. The Chile forward would join on an initial loan with an obligation to make his move permanent for €30m.
Palace have also reopened talks with Marseille over a deal for Netherlands defender Quentin Timber after confirming the signing of Honest Ahanor on loan from Atalanta earlier.
Forest have let a lot of players go out on loan, are they starting to look a bit thin. Glasner’s football is physically demanding. He wants intensity, running and aggressive pressing. You can’t really do that with all season without a bit of depth.
Got to say, so am I. Ever get a little inkling that a particular team with struggle/do well? I just have a sense that this might be a tricky campaign. But what do I know?
“The Premier League clubs have now spent upwards of three billion pounds on players this summer. I realize this sounds like a lot, but in today’s world that barely buys you a modern aircraft carrier. Heck, you could only afford ten frigates for that money,” so says Kári Tulinius.
As I said it before, Aston Villa needed to look at England U-21 defenders. They’re affordable and Aston Villa suit them. Here it is. Former England U-21 captain Taylor Harwood-Bellis is going to Aston Villa. That’s good for England if he is part of Thomas Tuchel’s England plan for the next Euro.
Then PG [just PG]:
Not sure if you’ve seen this yet: Chema Andrés to Brighton - DONE DEAL. Verbal agreement reached with VfB Stuttgart over a transfer for 21 y/o talented midfielder. Up to €23m all-in + sell-on. Chema on his way for medical.
Liverpool have confirmed they have a deal in place to sign Genk’s teenage goalkeeper Lucca Brughmans, with the 18-year-old due to arrive at Anfield next summer for a fee that could rise to £30m with add-ons.
The highly-rated keeper will remain at Genk on loan for the rest of this season. He has agreed a six-year contract with Liverpool, who have signed several young prospects this year as part of a strategy led by Matt Newberry at their global talent team.
St Etienne’s 18-year-old striker Djylian N’Guessan is expected to follow in a £4.3m deal. Brughmans, who impressed Liverpool’s scouts at the Uefa under-17 championship in Albania last summer, could come straight into the club’s first team picture next summer. Alisson is in the final year of his current contract and Giorgi Mamardashvili’s long-term future at Liverpool looks uncertain.
Another loan move from the Premier League to the Championship
Ben Fisher
Zach Abbott has signed a new four-year contract with Nottingham Forest and joined Southampton until the end of the season.
The 20-year-old academy graduate, who joined the club aged 11, made his top-flight debut last season and featured seven times as Forest reached the Europa League semi-finals.
“I had memorable experiences last year that have given me even more hunger to improve and continue my development,” said the defender, who is comfortable at centre-back and right-back.
“Laying out 225m on Bouaddi and Enzo doesn’t speak well to the 117m they spent on the (so far, unconvincing) Anderson. But what’s 350 million on midfielders in one window amongst friends?”
Another head scratcher, this one from Peter Mumola.
Leeds have agreed a deal with Eintracht Frankfurt to sign Jean-Mattéo Bahoya on an initial loan, with an option to make the France Under-21 forward’s move permanent for around £26m.
Daniel Farke’s side only have a few hours to complete all the paperwork but look to have got their man after missing out on Mykhailo Mudryk when he joined Spurs instead.
Jean-Matteo Bahoya playing for Frankfurt. Photograph: Marvin Ibo Guengoer/GES Sportfoto/Getty Images
Coventry have allowed Liam Kitching to join Sheffield United on loan for the season.
The 26-year-old defender was a regular en route to promotion as champions last campaign but has fallen down the pecking order following the arrivals of Aurele Amenda, Ethan Pinnock and Stephen Mfuni.
Kitching has not played a minute of Coventry’s opening two games in the Premier League, both of which ended in defeat. He started Coventry’s 4-2 win over Plymouth in the Carabao Cup and will now bolster Chris Wilder’s ranks in the second tier.
Nick Woltemade is bringing his unique fashion sense to Turin after completing a one year loan from Newcastle to Juventus.
The deal, which involves no obligation to buy, is costing the Serie A club around £3.5m.
Woltemade did not really fit into either Eddie Howe or Matias Jaissle’s high intensity style but the Germany forward - who cost Newcastle a record £69m this time last year - is immensely talented and Tynesiders will wish “Wolte-Wow” well.
Gary Naylor, an Everton fan and a good man, sets me straight on Beto:
Hi Daniel. Beto didn’t score many goals, but some were very important at a time when the club was fragile, tottering even. He is also a decent bloke who felt Everton in his heart and wasn’t afraid to show it. He goes with our best wishes and he’ll always be welcome at Hill Dickinson.
That’s lovely stuff. I hope you speak for all (or at least most) Toffee supporters.
Love this from Philip Midgley-Carver on the potential Fofana deal:
As a Palace fan, if there is a problem with the Sunderland plane then clearly Fofana should get on the Palace plane. Not our fault Sunderland sent a plane which hadn’t passed its MOT (or whatever the equivalent is for planes). Plus, I can assure him that the “Tasty Jerk” chicken place just outside Selhurst is, indeed, very tasty in case culinary options in South London might be the clincher for him.
“Why do you think no miserable Premier League side has gone for Harvey Elliott? Would be a good fit for a Palace, wouldn’t you think?”
Good question, Kevin Wilson.
My guess is that Liverpool wanted to keep him in case he comes good over the year. A season eating paella on the Mediterranean coast could see an upturn in his performances.
I know this is nothing new, but these numbers really make my skin crawl. How much did that leftback from Uruguay cost?
Well, there’s method to the madness, apparently, as Humphrey Elles-Hill (an Arsenal fan ‘proud of the club’s prudence)notes:
Hi Daniel. As much as it pains me, is the Blue Co business model starting to work? They seem to have inflated the market’s valuations of players so that they’re now seeing proper profits from wild buys like Enzo and poor performers like Delap?… are we going to see them sell Rodgers for £200m in a few years time, having won the premier league and mastered the Premier league’s flimsy economic structures? They were being written off as maverick charlatans who didn’t understand football not that long ago by this newspaper’s best writers!?
I don’t have them winning the title (still think Arsenal have enough to go back-to-back) but they are contenders, no doubt. Enough for second perhaps?
summary: Manchester City have agreed a £125m deal to sign Enzo Fernández from Chelsea and completed the signing of Iliman Nidaye from Everton for a fee rising to £65m. Meanwhile, clubs across Europe have been active on transfer deadline day, with Sunderland and Crystal Palace locked in a battle to sign Lyon's Malick Fofana, and several other loan and permanent moves finalized.
key_points: Manchester City agreed a £125m fixed fee deal to sign Enzo Fernández from Chelsea.
Manchester City completed the £65m signing of forward Iliman Nidaye from Everton on a five-year contract.
Sunderland and Crystal Palace engaged in a tug-of-war to sign Lyon winger Malick Fofana.
Everton's Beto and Nathan Patterson both secured permanent transfers to Italian clubs Fiorentina and Torino respectively.

title: Transfer deadline day live: Man City and Chelsea agree £125m Enzo Fernandez deal
author: Ji-Min Lee; Daniel Zeqiri; Matt Law; Dominic King; Sam Dean; James Ducker; Luke Edwards; John Percy; Mike McGrath
content:
![Enzo Fernandez is expected to reunite with Enzo Maresca at Manchester City](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/football/2026/09/01/TELEMMGLPICT000500313493_17882804108040_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bq4KdjWabbidXRBu7jUVums2_WH3fGO4ZFU7f6kLemkWM.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Enzo Fernandez is expected to reunite with Enzo Maresca at Manchester City](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/football/2026/09/01/TELEMMGLPICT000500313493_17882804108040_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bq4KdjWabbidXRBu7jUVums2_WH3fGO4ZFU7f6kLemkWM.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
Carragher: City now Arsenal’s main challengers
Speaking about the Enzo Fernández deal on Sky Sports, Carragher said: “It pushes them above Chelsea. Myself and plenty of others felt Chelsea would have a really good season, and I still believe that.
“A lot of that is on the back of no European football, having a new manager and the front three they have got.
“But losing Enzo Fernandez, who for me over the last two or three years has been one of the big players for Chelsea... they’ve always had five or six top players but maybe not a lot around them.
“They’ve let one of them go, to Man City, it’s a huge fee but City look a lot stronger now and I’d say they are going to be the main challengers to Arsenal.”
Chelsea willing to sell with no replacement guaranteed
Chelsea had been holding off from sanctioning Enzo Fernández’s move to Manchester City while they searched for a new midfielder of their own.
But City’s willingness to agree a £125m package has convinced Chelsea to give the green light to the Fernández move without any guarantees over an incoming signing.
Chelsea still have a few hours to try to make something happen, having had a bid for Lamine Camara turned down.
But Chelsea ultimately felt they had no choice but to let Fernández, who made it clear he wanted to leave, go in the best interests of the club.
Chelsea believe they have a strong squad, regardless of whether or not a new player is signed today, and will continue to weigh up their options.
![Enzo Maresca hugs Enzo Fernandez](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/football/2026/09/01/TELEMMGLPICT000498358154_17882793169360_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqqVzuuqpFlyLIwiB6NTmJwSX5rhseiWKOo9p9OQ-ymek.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Everton working to complete three signings
The medicals are under way for Jack Grealish, Ainsley Maitland-Niles and Folarin Balogun at Everton but there is no clarity on when all three deals will be concluded. It must be stressed that no issues are envisaged and they will be the only additions to the squad before the window closes. No further departures are expected, either.
On the other side of the city, things are winding down for Liverpool. Harvey Elliott’s loan to Valencia will be officially announced in due course. It is a straight loan, without an obligation to buy.
Deal agreed for Enzo Fernandez
Chelsea have agreed a £125m package to sell Enzo Fernández to Manchester City so the saga is finally coming to a close.
Chelsea will be happy with a fee that equals the British transfer record and City head coach Enzo Maresca will be delighted to land his top target.
It feels like a win-win all round as Fernández wanted to leave Chelsea and the club wanted over £120m after their initial deadline to do a deal expired.
It remains to be seen if Chelsea land any of their three main deadline day targets with a few hours of the window to go.
Chelsea had a bid rejected for Lamine Camara, Roma have not been playing ball on Manu Kone and the identity of the mystery Premier League target has not yet emerged.
Newcastle have two bits of business to tick off
Newcastle insist the only deals they are working on for the rest of the day are the departures of Nick Woltemade on loan to Juventus and Sean Neave to Wolverhampton Wanderers.
Multiple sources deny there is any chance of Jacob Murphy leaving for Nottingham Forest despite claims of a second bid being rejected today.
summary: Manchester City and Chelsea have agreed a £125m deal for Enzo Fernández, allowing the midfielder to reunite with manager Enzo Maresca. Chelsea opted to sell the player, who made it clear he wanted to leave, without a guaranteed replacement lined up before the deadline. Meanwhile, Everton are working on medicals for Jack Grealish, Ainsley Maitland-Niles, and Folarin Balogun.
key_points: Manchester City and Chelsea agreed to a £125m package for Enzo Fernández.
Chelsea let Fernández leave without a guaranteed replacement, though a bid for Lamine Camara was rejected.
Jamie Carragher believes the signing makes Manchester City the main challengers to Arsenal.
Everton are conducting medicals for Jack Grealish, Ainsley Maitland-Niles, and Folarin Balogun.
Harvey Elliott is set to join Valencia on a straight loan from Liverpool.

title: Transfer news LIVE: Deadline Day latest deals and updates - Crystal Palace could hijack Sunderland's Malick Fofana deal, Everton eye Ainsley Maitland Niles
author: Live Reporting Jude Winter; Tasnim Chowdhury; Flora Snelson; Freya Sweet; Tyrese King; Grace Wheeler
content:
Teenager Honest Ahanor will join Chelsea next season, but the Atalanta defender will play the rest of this campaign on loan at Crystal Palace.
The Blues have agreed a deal worth up to Â£40m for the 18-year-old Italy international.
But he will not arrive at Stamford Bridge immediately and will instead join Palace before officially becoming a Chelsea player next summer
